Node identifies the tooling ecosystem, not a confirmed production Node server. Bun is explicitly declared as the package manager; the Cloudflare Vite plugin, workers directory, Wrangler configuration, and deployment script indicate a Cloudflare Workers deployment target.
Keep the candidate at high confidence: its canonical fields match the deterministic base, and its added explanations are supported by the supplied evidence.

Use the existing MLAI article system at `/articles`, React Router 7, React 19, TypeScript `.tsx`, Tailwind and Bun 1.3.5. Its published articles are the visual reference. Preserve the site shell, registry, route metadata, analytics, accessibility and all published download assets. Article content lives under `app/articles/content/`; use the approved target directory and filename, and inspect a neighbouring published article and its registration in `app/articles/registry.ts` before matching its export structure. Do not invent a route, registry entry shape or layout props: the supplied excerpts do not establish those contracts.

Reuse the current article component library and its actual exports and props; do not introduce dependencies or a parallel scaffold. Use the `~/` alias: named imports include `{ ArticleHeroHeader }` from `"~/components/articles/ArticleHeroHeader"`, `{ ArticleCallout }` from `"~/components/articles/ArticleCallout"` and `{ ArticleFAQ }` from `"~/components/articles/ArticleFAQ"`; `ArticleCompanyCTA` is the default export from `"~/components/articles/ArticleCompanyCTA"`. Use React Router links imported from `"react-router"` with `to`, not Next.js APIs or client/server directives. `ArticleCallout` accepts `title`, `variant` (`"info"`, `"success"`, `"warning"` or `"brand"`) and children; `ArticleFAQ` accepts `items` containing `question` and `answer`, with optional `anchorId` and `heading`. Do not import the missing `ArticleResourceDownload` or `ArticleSummaryCard`. Use the verified resource components only with their documented props and approved, working asset URLs.

Prefer clear Australian English, researched claims, labelled uncertainty, practical examples and an approved audience/action. Respect narrow and wide layouts and existing component styling, including `text-gray-900`, `text-gray-700`, `border-gray-200`, `rounded-2xl` and `my-12`; do not invent design tokens. Preserve the verified layout/header composition: `ArticleHeroHeader` renders the single h1 when used; never duplicate a title, breadcrumb or author section already rendered by the layout. Preserve route-owned canonical/social/schema metadata without adding competing metadata or structured data. Keep heading hierarchy, TOC anchors, comment slot IDs and resource links stable across revisions. Use meaningful image alternatives and a horizontally scrollable region for wide tables.

An optional resource or company CTA must match the approved article brief. `ArticleCompanyCTA` requires `title`, `body`, `buttonText` and `buttonHref`; keep CTA wording generic and verify its destination. Do not add service chips or unsolicited disclaimers or warnings. Never change existing published content as a side effect of generating a new article. Keep browser-only work out of server rendering; any effect cleanup must return void. Validate with the repository’s existing Bun scripts, including `bun run typecheck` and `bun run build`, without changing dependencies or build configuration to mask failures. The exact frozen build, registered listing/detail routes, required assets, real 404 and artifact marker are release gates, not presentation flags; verify their existing contracts before release rather than inventing missing integration details.

It brings together founders, builders, learners and industry partners through practical events, workshops, hackathons, founder tools and community connections. MLAI also operates MLAI Studio, a paid AI and software delivery service.

**Type:** Not-for-profit community with founder-focused programs, software tools and a paid project delivery service.  
**Founded:** [To be filled]  
**Location/Market:** Australia-wide, based in Melbourne. Events and activities include Melbourne, Sydney and online options; availability varies by program.

**Naming:** Use **MLAI** in general editorial copy. The website also uses **MLAI Aus** and identifies the organisation as **MLAI Aus Inc.** on its contact page.

---

## 2. Mission & North Star

**Mission Statement:**  
Help Australians learn, build and start companies in the AI era by making AI practical, accessible and fun.

**Vision/North Star:**  
Help get **1,000 Australian startups off the ground by 2030**, with a focus on AI-enabled companies, stronger local capability and more high-complexity exports.

This is a mission target, not a claim that 1,000 startups have already launched.

**Key Values:**  
The following are editorial interpretations of the website’s positioning, rather than a formally published values list:

- **Community first:** Create useful connections and recognise meaningful contributions.
- **Practical participation:** Help people move from learning to prototypes, teams and real products.
- **Accessibility:** Welcome people with different technical skills and professional backgrounds.
- **Evidence and accountability:** Build reporting and content from approved company evidence, make gaps visible and retain human review.
- **Australian capability:** Support local founders, builders and the wider Australian AI ecosystem.

---

## 3. Target Audience

### Primary Audience

Use this company as the “home base” in articles for readers such as:

- **Aspiring and early-stage Australian founders:** People validating a problem, building an MVP, finding collaborators and preparing to launch an AI-enabled business.
- **AI builders and practitioners:** Developers, AI engineers, data scientists and software builders seeking practical projects, peer learning, mentors and potential paid work.
- **AI learners and career changers:** Students, newcomers and professionals seeking plain-English explanations, learning pathways and welcoming ways to participate.
- **Small-business owners and startup operators:** People with repetitive administration, disconnected systems or a software idea who need help deciding what to improve or build.

**Secondary audiences:**

- Investors, VCs and portfolio teams seeking connections with founders and builders.
- Sponsors, universities, government and industry organisations supporting Australian AI capability.
- Clinicians, designers, researchers and other domain specialists contributing to interdisciplinary projects.
- Volunteers who want to support events, help founders and take on community responsibilities.

### Pain Points to Address

- Uncertainty about where to start with AI or which learning and community options are useful.
- Difficulty turning an idea into a focused, testable product.
- Limited access to collaborators, technical feedback and professional connections.
- Repetitive work, fragmented business systems and hard-to-find company information.
- Difficulty producing credible investor updates and consistent marketing from reliable evidence.
- Uncertainty about project scope, cost, privacy, ownership and ongoing support.
- For builders, difficulty finding clearly scoped paid projects that fit their skills and availability.

### Goals They’re Trying to Achieve

- Learn through practical participation rather than theory alone.
- Validate a customer problem and build something people can test.
- Find peers, collaborators, mentors and useful introductions.
- Launch and grow an Australian startup.
- Communicate progress clearly to customers, communities and investors.
- Improve business workflows with appropriate software and human oversight.
- Demonstrate delivery capability through real projects.

---

## 4. Product/Service Offerings

Think of MLAI’s offering as a community-supported pathway from learning and connection to building and launching—not as a single software product.

### Core Offerings

1. **Events, workshops and hackathons**  
   Meetups, build sessions, networking, practical workshops and themed hackathons. Topics include AI engineering, healthcare, energy and startup building. Check individual organiser pages for dates, locations, admission and online ticket options.

2. **Community-written articles**  
   Plain-English guides covering AI, machine learning, data science careers, startup development and Australian technology pathways.

3. **MLAI community access: MLAI Chat and Slack**  
   One community with multiple ways to participate. MLAI Chat supports web, desktop, iPhone and Android access; approved public channels can bridge to Slack. An MLAI invite or approved membership is required. Bridge coverage is operator-managed and can change during the pilot.

4. **Founder Tools**  
   Tools for organising company context and communicating from approved evidence:
   - **Vibe Raising:** Assemble evidence, review recorded progress and approve monthly founder updates before sharing.
   - **Vibe Marketing:** Research topics, prepare content and monitor published performance using approved company evidence.
   - **Shared company profile:** Maintain consistent company context across workflows.

   Creating or opening a Founder Tools workspace requires an MLAI account.

5. **Vibe Coding and Vibe Coworking**  
   The homepage describes hands-on AI-assisted building from zero to MVP, community feature bounties and coworking for MLAI volunteers across Australian capitals. Confirm current participation requirements and availability before promoting a specific opportunity.

6. **MLAI Studio: paid AI and software delivery**  
   Australian builders help businesses scope and deliver AI workflows, agents, automations, integrations, search tools and MVPs. Studio checks whether existing software can solve the problem before recommending a custom build. Entry points include a free 15-minute chat with Sam and a project brief.

7. **MLAI Studio builder network**  
   Builders apply, undergo human review and may be matched to scoped, paid projects. Matching depends on skills, availability and project fit; joining the pool does not guarantee work.

8. **Roo and Roo Points**  
   Roo is MLAI’s Slack helper for contribution recognition, rewards, coworking and requests. Roo Points are an internal thank-you system redeemable for eligible community perks, subject to availability and applicable rules.

9. **Sponsorship and volunteering**  
   Organisations can discuss supporting MLAI’s activities; individuals can contribute through events and community tasks.

### Key Differentiators

These are supported positioning points, not claims of exclusive market superiority:

- **A community-to-company pathway:** Connects learning, participation, prototypes, founder support and project delivery.
- **Australian focus:** Local founders, Australian builders and connections across startups, universities, government and industry.
- **Practical, multidisciplinary participation:** Welcomes technical practitioners alongside clinicians, designers, students and operators.
- **Evidence-first founder workflows:** Source visibility, explicit evidence gaps and approval before sharing.
- **Pragmatic project scoping:** Studio considers existing tools before proposing new software, with scope and commercial terms agreed before paid work begins.
- **Contribution-based participation:** Roo recognises useful community work rather than treating membership as passive access.

**Value proposition:**  
MLAI helps Australians turn interest in AI into useful skills, stronger connections, real products and startup progress—with tools and paid delivery support where appropriate.

---

## 5. Proof Points & Credibility

**Trust Signals (pick 1–2 per article, max):**

- The press kit reports a community of **12,000+ people**.
- The press kit says regular events attract **100–300 attendees**.
- The homepage says events have been sponsored and supported by **more than 50 organisations across Australia**.
- HealthHack is presented with **UNSW No Code Society**, bringing healthcare and technical participants together.
- MLAI Studio presents MLAI’s own tools—including Vibe Raising, Vibe Marketing and Watt the Hack—as examples of its work.
- The builder page describes mentoring from people with experience at **Canva, Atlassian and MIT**.

**Evidence-handling notes:**

- Attribute figures to MLAI’s website or press kit and verify them before publication when currency matters.
- The HealthHack page says **10,000+ members**, while the press kit says **12,000+ people**. Prefer the press-kit figure for general company descriptions, while retaining its wording and attribution. Do not combine these into a growth-rate claim.
- Named event collaborations do not establish organisation-wide endorsement.
- Awards, certifications and independently verified performance results: **[To be filled]**.

**What NOT to claim:**

- That MLAI has already launched 1,000 startups.
- That MLAI is objectively Australia’s largest, best or leading AI community without comparative evidence.
- Guaranteed investment, investor introductions, employment, project matches or startup success.
- That mentor experience at Canva, Atlassian or MIT means those organisations endorse or partner with MLAI.
- That MLAI’s internal software examples are external client case studies.
- That all events are free, online, open-access or currently available.
- That Roo Points are wages, money, an investment or a guaranteed route to paid work.
- That community software is fully Slack-synchronised, end-to-end encrypted or covered by a security certification not established in the supplied content.
- Guaranteed search rankings, answer-engine visibility, productivity gains or clinical outcomes.
- That hackathon prototypes are validated healthcare products.

---

## 6. CTA Guidance

### How to Describe the Company in One Line (choose one per article)

- “MLAI is a Melbourne-based not-for-profit helping Australians learn, build and launch startups in the AI era.”
- “MLAI brings Australian founders, builders and learners together through practical AI events, tools and community.”
- For service-focused articles: “MLAI Studio is MLAI’s paid AI and software delivery service, connecting businesses with Australian builders.”

### Primary CTAs (Use ONE per article, aligned to topic)

**For beginners/learners:**
> “Find an MLAI event that fits what you want to learn or build.”  
> Target: https://mlai.au/events

**For builders/practitioners:**
> “Apply to the MLAI Studio builder pool for potential matches with scoped, paid projects.”  
> Target: https://mlai.au/mlai-studio/build-with-us

For community participation rather than paid-work intent, use:
> “Explore MLAI’s community access options.”  
> Target: https://mlai.au/community

**For decision-makers/leaders:**
> “Tell MLAI Studio what you want to improve so the team can review the fit and help scope the work.”  
> Target: https://mlai.au/mlai-studio/start-project

For readers who need an introductory conversation, link to https://mlai.au/mlai-studio and its free 15-minute chat.

**For partners/sponsors:**
> “Explore a sponsorship partnership supporting Australia’s AI community.”  
> Target: https://mlai.au/sponsors

**For founders using evidence and communication tools:**
> “Explore Founder Tools for evidence-based updates and marketing workflows.”  
> Target: https://mlai.au/founder-tools/start

### Verified Pages to Link To

| Reader need | Page |
|---|---|
| Learn through guides | `/articles` |
| Attend an event | `/events` |
| Explore hackathons | `/hackathons` |
| Access the community | `/community` |
| Understand Roo and contribution rewards | `/roo` |

| Verify company boilerplate and assets | `/press-kit` |

Do not invent dedicated product routes, booking URLs, Slack invitations or article slugs.

### CTA Rules

- Use **one primary CTA per article**, as a relevant aside or final line.
- Match the action to the reader’s immediate need—not merely the article’s keyword.
- Keep the article useful without requiring registration or purchase.
- Distinguish community participation, founder software and paid Studio delivery.
- State material conditions where relevant: application, approval, account requirement, availability or paid service.
- Supporting resource links are acceptable; do not turn them into repeated promotional CTAs.

### What NOT to Do with CTAs

- Do not promise “Get funded”, “Get hired” or “Launch successfully”.
- Do not promote free custom development; Studio project work is paid.
- Do not imply that joining Slack automatically grants unrestricted MLAI Chat access.
- Do not invent urgency, limited places, discounts or current event availability.
- Do not use the builder application for businesses seeking project delivery.

---

## 7. Tone & Voice Guidelines

**Brand Voice:** Practical, welcoming, builder-friendly and community-first, with light Australian informality and occasional playfulness.

### Tone Attributes

- **Action-oriented:** Explain what readers can try, test, build or review next.
- **Accessible:** Use plain English without sacrificing technical accuracy.
- **Evidence-led:** Separate facts, assumptions, recorded results and unresolved gaps.
- **Collaborative:** Emphasise learning together and making useful contributions.
- **Lightly playful:** The Roo mascot and “pirate ship” language allow personality, but should not dominate editorial content.
- **Calm about AI:** Focus on appropriate applications and measurable outcomes rather than hype.

### Do’s

- Use **Australian English**: “organisation”, “recognise”, “optimise” and “centre”.
- Use specific tasks and examples: a small admin workflow, a first prototype or a monthly founder update.
- Explain technical terms and acronyms on first use.
- Prefer “builders”, “founders”, “community”, “practical”, “prototype” and “meaningful contribution”.
- Preserve product names: **MLAI Studio**, **Founder Tools**, **Vibe Raising**, **Vibe Marketing**, **MLAI Chat**, **Roo** and **Roo Points**.
- Use “not-for-profit” for consistent company descriptions.
- Preserve human judgement, review and approval in descriptions of AI workflows.
- Use A$ where Australian-dollar amounts could otherwise be ambiguous.

### Don’ts

- Avoid inflated language such as “revolutionary”, “guaranteed”, “effortless success” or “the ultimate solution”.
- Do not imply AI removes the need for testing, privacy review or domain expertise.
- Do not frame founders and learners as needing elite technical credentials to participate.
- Avoid forced slang, excessive pirate references or mascot-heavy explanations.
- Do not treat “vibe coding” as a reason to skip evaluation, security or maintainability.
- Do not describe volunteer participation as employment or Roo Points as remuneration.
- Do not turn general education into an unsolicited sales pitch.

---

## 8. Writing Guidance Summary

### Language Conventions

- **Locale:** Australian English.
- **Preferred terms:** MLAI; not-for-profit AI community; Australian founders; builders; practical AI; founder updates; approved evidence; scoped paid projects; meaningful contribution.
- **Avoided terms:** Unsubstantiated superlatives, guaranteed outcomes, investment promises and language presenting community rewards as money.

### Content Rules

1. **Lead with the reader’s task.** Provide actionable steps, useful examples and clear limitations before introducing MLAI.
2. **Keep the mission distinct from achievement.** The 1,000-startup figure is a target for 2030.
3. **Keep offerings distinct.** Founder Tools organises and communicates evidence; Studio scopes and builds systems; community programs provide learning and connection.
4. **Research external claims.** Verify Australian regulations, accelerator terms, course details, investment information and event logistics with suitable sources.
5. **Do not treat scraped dates as current.** Confirm event status and publication metadata before using time-sensitive wording.
6. **Label uncertainty.** Do not invent founder biographies, launch dates, pricing, participant outcomes, testimonials or product capabilities.
7. **Use low-risk examples.** Prefer fictional or appropriately de-identified data and measurable pilot outcomes. Do not encourage readers to upload sensitive data without approval.
8. **Respect commercial boundaries.** Studio timelines, support, ownership and costs depend on the proposal. Australian builders do not automatically mean Australian-only data processing.
9. **Describe Studio terms accurately when relevant.** The advertised monthly package includes 40 builder hours; scoping, meetings, testing and coordination may count towards that allocation. Hosting, AI usage and paid software are extra unless included in the proposal.
10. **Keep rewards separate from work guarantees.** Roo Points can recognise contribution and support consideration for opportunities, but do not guarantee roles or paid projects.
11. **Treat missing information as a publication requirement.** Use **[To be filled]** rather than inventing missing facts or approvals.

### Implementation Boundaries for AI-Generated Articles

- Reuse the existing React Router article system, components and publishing contracts; do not create a parallel scaffold.
- Inspect neighbouring published modules, the reader route and registry before implementation.
- Preserve approved audience/action identifiers, metadata, analytics, accessibility and download assets.
- Do not invent authors, publication dates, component props, routes or asset URLs.
- The supplied brand context is incomplete and contains a styling-stack inconsistency: the design guide references Tailwind, while `tech_stack` marks it as false. Verify the repository rather than resolving this by assumption.
- Brand colour values, font names and complete integration contracts: **[To be filled from verified site assets or repository]**.

# Company Overview: MLAI

> This document provides context for AI-generated articles. It ensures content aligns with the company's brand, audience, and goals.

---

## 1. Company Identity

**What we are (plain-English):**  
MLAI is a Melbourne-based, volunteer-led, not-for-profit AI community helping Australians learn, build and launch startups. It brings together founders, builders, learners and industry partners through practical events, workshops, hackathons, founder tools and community connections. MLAI also operates MLAI Studio, a paid AI and software delivery service.

**Industry/Sector:** Artificial intelligence, machine learning, startup development and community education.  
**Type:** Not-for-profit community with founder-focused programs, software tools and a paid project delivery service.  
**Founded:** [To be filled]  
**Location/Market:** Australia-wide, based in Melbourne. Events and activities include Melbourne, Sydney and online options; availability varies by program.

**Naming:** Use **MLAI** in general editorial copy. The website also uses **MLAI Aus** and identifies the organisation as **MLAI Aus Inc.** on its contact page.

---

## 2. Mission & North Star

**Mission Statement:**  
Help Australians learn, build and start companies in the AI era by making AI practical, accessible and fun.

**Vision/North Star:**  
Help get **1,000 Australian startups off the ground by 2030**, with a focus on AI-enabled companies, stronger local capability and more high-complexity exports.

This is a mission target, not a claim that 1,000 startups have already launched.

**Key Values:**  
The following are editorial interpretations of the website’s positioning, rather than a formally published values list:

- **Community first:** Create useful connections and recognise meaningful contributions.
- **Practical participation:** Help people move from learning to prototypes, teams and real products.
- **Accessibility:** Welcome people with different technical skills and professional backgrounds.
- **Evidence and accountability:** Build reporting and content from approved company evidence, make gaps visible and retain human review.
- **Australian capability:** Support local founders, builders and the wider Australian AI ecosystem.

---

## 3. Target Audience

### Primary Audience

Use this company as the “home base” in articles for readers such as:

- **Aspiring and early-stage Australian founders:** People validating a problem, building an MVP, finding collaborators and preparing to launch an AI-enabled business.
- **AI builders and practitioners:** Developers, AI engineers, data scientists and software builders seeking practical projects, peer learning, mentors and potential paid work.
- **AI learners and career changers:** Students, newcomers and professionals seeking plain-English explanations, learning pathways and welcoming ways to participate.
- **Small-business owners and startup operators:** People with repetitive administration, disconnected systems or a software idea who need help deciding what to improve or build.

**Secondary audiences:**

- Investors, VCs and portfolio teams seeking connections with founders and builders.
- Sponsors, universities, government and industry organisations supporting Australian AI capability.
- Clinicians, designers, researchers and other domain specialists contributing to interdisciplinary projects.
- Volunteers who want to support events, help founders and take on community responsibilities.

### Pain Points to Address

- Uncertainty about where to start with AI or which learning and community options are useful.
- Difficulty turning an idea into a focused, testable product.
- Limited access to collaborators, technical feedback and professional connections.
- Repetitive work, fragmented business systems and hard-to-find company information.
- Difficulty producing credible investor updates and consistent marketing from reliable evidence.
- Uncertainty about project scope, cost, privacy, ownership and ongoing support.
- For builders, difficulty finding clearly scoped paid projects that fit their skills and availability.

### Goals They’re Trying to Achieve

- Learn through practical participation rather than theory alone.
- Validate a customer problem and build something people can test.
- Find peers, collaborators, mentors and useful introductions.
- Launch and grow an Australian startup.
- Communicate progress clearly to customers, communities and investors.
- Improve business workflows with appropriate software and human oversight.
- Demonstrate delivery capability through real projects.

---

## 4. Product/Service Offerings

Think of MLAI’s offering as a community-supported pathway from learning and connection to building and launching—not as a single software product.

### Core Offerings

1. **Events, workshops and hackathons**  
   Meetups, build sessions, networking, practical workshops and themed hackathons. Topics include AI engineering, healthcare, energy and startup building. Check individual organiser pages for dates, locations, admission and online ticket options.

2. **Community-written articles**  
   Plain-English guides covering AI, machine learning, data science careers, startup development and Australian technology pathways.

3. **MLAI community access: MLAI Chat and Slack**  
   One community with multiple ways to participate. MLAI Chat supports web, desktop, iPhone and Android access; approved public channels can bridge to Slack. An MLAI invite or approved membership is required. Bridge coverage is operator-managed and can change during the pilot.

4. **Founder Tools**  
   Tools for organising company context and communicating from approved evidence:
   - **Vibe Raising:** Assemble evidence, review recorded progress and approve monthly founder updates before sharing.
   - **Vibe Marketing:** Research topics, prepare content and monitor published performance using approved company evidence.
   - **Shared company profile:** Maintain consistent company context across workflows.

   Creating or opening a Founder Tools workspace requires an MLAI account.

5. **Vibe Coding and Vibe Coworking**  
   The homepage describes hands-on AI-assisted building from zero to MVP, community feature bounties and coworking for MLAI volunteers across Australian capitals. Confirm current participation requirements and availability before promoting a specific opportunity.

6. **MLAI Studio: paid AI and software delivery**  
   Australian builders help businesses scope and deliver AI workflows, agents, automations, integrations, search tools and MVPs. Studio checks whether existing software can solve the problem before recommending a custom build. Entry points include a free 15-minute chat with Sam and a project brief.

7. **MLAI Studio builder network**  
   Builders apply, undergo human review and may be matched to scoped, paid projects. Matching depends on skills, availability and project fit; joining the pool does not guarantee work.

8. **Roo and Roo Points**  
   Roo is MLAI’s Slack helper for contribution recognition, rewards, coworking and requests. Roo Points are an internal thank-you system redeemable for eligible community perks, subject to availability and applicable rules.

9. **Sponsorship and volunteering**  
   Organisations can discuss supporting MLAI’s activities; individuals can contribute through events and community tasks.

### Key Differentiators

These are supported positioning points, not claims of exclusive market superiority:

- **A community-to-company pathway:** Connects learning, participation, prototypes, founder support and project delivery.
- **Australian focus:** Local founders, Australian builders and connections across startups, universities, government and industry.
- **Practical, multidisciplinary participation:** Welcomes technical practitioners alongside clinicians, designers, students and operators.
- **Evidence-first founder workflows:** Source visibility, explicit evidence gaps and approval before sharing.
- **Pragmatic project scoping:** Studio considers existing tools before proposing new software, with scope and commercial terms agreed before paid work begins.
- **Contribution-based participation:** Roo recognises useful community work rather than treating membership as passive access.

**Value proposition:**  
MLAI helps Australians turn interest in AI into useful skills, stronger connections, real products and startup progress—with tools and paid delivery support where appropriate.

---

## 5. Proof Points & Credibility

**Trust Signals (pick 1–2 per article, max):**

- The press kit reports a community of **12,000+ people**.
- The press kit says regular events attract **100–300 attendees**.
- The homepage says events have been sponsored and supported by **more than 50 organisations across Australia**.
- HealthHack is presented with **UNSW No Code Society**, bringing healthcare and technical participants together.
- MLAI Studio presents MLAI’s own tools—including Vibe Raising, Vibe Marketing and Watt the Hack—as examples of its work.
- The builder page describes mentoring from people with experience at **Canva, Atlassian and MIT**.

**Evidence-handling notes:**

- Attribute figures to MLAI’s website or press kit and verify them before publication when currency matters.
- The HealthHack page says **10,000+ members**, while the press kit says **12,000+ people**. Prefer the press-kit figure for general company descriptions, while retaining its wording and attribution. Do not combine these into a growth-rate claim.
- Named event collaborations do not establish organisation-wide endorsement.
- Awards, certifications and independently verified performance results: **[To be filled]**.

**What NOT to claim:**

- That MLAI has already launched 1,000 startups.
- That MLAI is objectively Australia’s largest, best or leading AI community without comparative evidence.
- Guaranteed investment, investor introductions, employment, project matches or startup success.
- That mentor experience at Canva, Atlassian or MIT means those organisations endorse or partner with MLAI.
- That MLAI’s internal software examples are external client case studies.
- That all events are free, online, open-access or currently available.
- That Roo Points are wages, money, an investment or a guaranteed route to paid work.
- That community software is fully Slack-synchronised, end-to-end encrypted or covered by a security certification not established in the supplied content.
- Guaranteed search rankings, answer-engine visibility, productivity gains or clinical outcomes.
- That hackathon prototypes are validated healthcare products.

---

## 6. CTA Guidance

### How to Describe the Company in One Line (choose one per article)

- “MLAI is a Melbourne-based not-for-profit helping Australians learn, build and launch startups in the AI era.”
- “MLAI brings Australian founders, builders and learners together through practical AI events, tools and community.”
- For service-focused articles: “MLAI Studio is MLAI’s paid AI and software delivery service, connecting businesses with Australian builders.”

### Primary CTAs (Use ONE per article, aligned to topic)

**For beginners/learners:**
> “Find an MLAI event that fits what you want to learn or build.”  
> Target: https://mlai.au/events

**For builders/practitioners:**
> “Apply to the MLAI Studio builder pool for potential matches with scoped, paid projects.”  
> Target: https://mlai.au/mlai-studio/build-with-us

For community participation rather than paid-work intent, use:
> “Explore MLAI’s community access options.”  
> Target: https://mlai.au/community

**For decision-makers/leaders:**
> “Tell MLAI Studio what you want to improve so the team can review the fit and help scope the work.”  
> Target: https://mlai.au/mlai-studio/start-project

For readers who need an introductory conversation, link to https://mlai.au/mlai-studio and its free 15-minute chat.

**For partners/sponsors:**
> “Explore a sponsorship partnership supporting Australia’s AI community.”  
> Target: https://mlai.au/sponsors

**For founders using evidence and communication tools:**
> “Explore Founder Tools for evidence-based updates and marketing workflows.”  
> Target: https://mlai.au/founder-tools/start

### Verified Pages to Link To

| Reader need | Page |
|---|---|
| Learn through guides | `/articles` |
| Attend an event | `/events` |
| Explore hackathons | `/hackathons` |
| Access the community | `/community` |
| Understand Roo and contribution rewards | `/roo` |
| Explore Founder Tools | `/founder-tools/start` |
| Review Vibe Raising | `/vibe-raising` |
| Explore paid delivery support | `/mlai-studio` |
| Submit a project brief | `/mlai-studio/start-project` |
| Apply as a builder | `/mlai-studio/build-with-us` |
| Discuss sponsorship | `/sponsors` |
| General or volunteer enquiries | `/contact` |
| Verify company boilerplate and assets | `/press-kit` |

Do not invent dedicated product routes, booking URLs, Slack invitations or article slugs.

### CTA Rules

- Use **one primary CTA per article**, as a relevant aside or final line.
- Match the action to the reader’s immediate need—not merely the article’s keyword.
- Keep the article useful without requiring registration or purchase.
- Distinguish community participation, founder software and paid Studio delivery.
- State material conditions where relevant: application, approval, account requirement, availability or paid service.
- Supporting resource links are acceptable; do not turn them into repeated promotional CTAs.

### What NOT to Do with CTAs

- Do not promise “Get funded”, “Get hired” or “Launch successfully”.
- Do not promote free custom development; Studio project work is paid.
- Do not imply that joining Slack automatically grants unrestricted MLAI Chat access.
- Do not invent urgency, limited places, discounts or current event availability.
- Do not use the builder application for businesses seeking project delivery.

---

## 7. Tone & Voice Guidelines

**Brand Voice:** Practical, welcoming, builder-friendly and community-first, with light Australian informality and occasional playfulness.

### Tone Attributes

- **Action-oriented:** Explain what readers can try, test, build or review next.
- **Accessible:** Use plain English without sacrificing technical accuracy.
- **Evidence-led:** Separate facts, assumptions, recorded results and unresolved gaps.
- **Collaborative:** Emphasise learning together and making useful contributions.
- **Lightly playful:** The Roo mascot and “pirate ship” language allow personality, but should not dominate editorial content.
- **Calm about AI:** Focus on appropriate applications and measurable outcomes rather than hype.

### Do’s

- Use **Australian English**: “organisation”, “recognise”, “optimise” and “centre”.
- Use specific tasks and examples: a small admin workflow, a first prototype or a monthly founder update.
- Explain technical terms and acronyms on first use.
- Prefer “builders”, “founders”, “community”, “practical”, “prototype” and “meaningful contribution”.
- Preserve product names: **MLAI Studio**, **Founder Tools**, **Vibe Raising**, **Vibe Marketing**, **MLAI Chat**, **Roo** and **Roo Points**.
- Use “not-for-profit” for consistent company descriptions.
- Preserve human judgement, review and approval in descriptions of AI workflows.
- Use A$ where Australian-dollar amounts could otherwise be ambiguous.

### Don’ts

- Avoid inflated language such as “revolutionary”, “guaranteed”, “effortless success” or “the ultimate solution”.
- Do not imply AI removes the need for testing, privacy review or domain expertise.
- Do not frame founders and learners as needing elite technical credentials to participate.
- Avoid forced slang, excessive pirate references or mascot-heavy explanations.
- Do not treat “vibe coding” as a reason to skip evaluation, security or maintainability.
- Do not describe volunteer participation as employment or Roo Points as remuneration.
- Do not turn general education into an unsolicited sales pitch.

---

## 8. Writing Guidance Summary

### Language Conventions

- **Locale:** Australian English.
- **Preferred terms:** MLAI; not-for-profit AI community; Australian founders; builders; practical AI; founder updates; approved evidence; scoped paid projects; meaningful contribution.
- **Avoided terms:** Unsubstantiated superlatives, guaranteed outcomes, investment promises and language presenting community rewards as money.

### Content Rules

1. **Lead with the reader’s task.** Provide actionable steps, useful examples and clear limitations before introducing MLAI.
2. **Keep the mission distinct from achievement.** The 1,000-startup figure is a target for 2030.
3. **Keep offerings distinct.** Founder Tools organises and communicates evidence; Studio scopes and builds systems; community programs provide learning and connection.
4. **Research external claims.** Verify Australian regulations, accelerator terms, course details, investment information and event logistics with suitable sources.
5. **Do not treat scraped dates as current.** Confirm event status and publication metadata before using time-sensitive wording.
6. **Label uncertainty.** Do not invent founder biographies, launch dates, pricing, participant outcomes, testimonials or product capabilities.
7. **Use low-risk examples.** Prefer fictional or appropriately de-identified data and measurable pilot outcomes. Do not encourage readers to upload sensitive data without approval.
8. **Respect commercial boundaries.** Studio timelines, support, ownership and costs depend on the proposal. Australian builders do not automatically mean Australian-only data processing.
9. **Describe Studio terms accurately when relevant.** The advertised monthly package includes 40 builder hours; scoping, meetings, testing and coordination may count towards that allocation. Hosting, AI usage and paid software are extra unless included in the proposal.
10. **Keep rewards separate from work guarantees.** Roo Points can recognise contribution and support consideration for opportunities, but do not guarantee roles or paid projects.
11. **Treat missing information as a publication requirement.** Use **[To be filled]** rather than inventing missing facts or approvals.

### Implementation Boundaries for AI-Generated Articles

- Reuse the existing React Router article system, components and publishing contracts; do not create a parallel scaffold.
- Inspect neighbouring published modules, the reader route and registry before implementation.
- Preserve approved audience/action identifiers, metadata, analytics, accessibility and download assets.
- Do not invent authors, publication dates, component props, routes or asset URLs.
- The supplied brand context is incomplete and contains a styling-stack inconsistency: the design guide references Tailwind, while `tech_stack` marks it as false. Verify the repository rather than resolving this by assumption.
- Brand colour values, font names and complete integration contracts: **[To be filled from verified site assets or repository]**.

article_system.reason: Repository exposes React Router article routes backed by TSX article component files under a stable content directory.

design_guide.seed_content: Use the existing MLAI article system at /articles, React Router 7, Tailwind and Bun 1.3.5. Its published articles are the visual reference. Preserve the site shell, registry, route metadata, analytics, accessibility and all published download assets. Reuse the current article component library and its actual props; do not introduce dependencies or a parallel scaffold. Prefer clear Australian English, researched claims, labelled uncertainty, practical examples and an approved audience/action. Respect narrow and wide layouts. ArticleHeroHeader owns the single h1; the route owns canonical/social/schema metadata. Keep heading hierarchy, TOC anchors, comment slot IDs and resource links stable across revisions. Use meaningful image alternatives and a scrollable region for wide tables. An optional resource or company CTA must match the approved article brief. Never change existing published content as a side effect of generating a new article. The exact frozen build, registered listing/detail routes, required assets, real 404 and artifact marker are release gates, not presentation flags.

article_template.seed_content:
Write an original, researched MLAI article about {{TOPIC}} as a React Router 7 TSX content module. Match the existing article library rather than creating a second publishing system.

The reviewed target is app/articles/content/featured/{slug}.tsx and /articles/featured/{slug}. The reader route owns ArticleLayout, canonical and social metadata, analytics and the surrounding site shell. Do not create routes, layouts, HTML documents or duplicate JSON-LD. Export a default React component and useCustomHeader=true when using ArticleHeroHeader. Export CATEGORY="featured", SLUG, DATE_PUBLISHED, DATE_MODIFIED, DESCRIPTION and FEATURED_FOCUS. Use factual metadata from the approved article brief. Preserve any approved editorial audience/action IDs and versions.

Use actual existing components with their existing import/export shapes:
- Named ArticleHeroHeader from ~/components/articles/ArticleHeroHeader. Props: title, titleHighlight?, breadcrumbs?, headerBgColor (cyan|purple|blue|orange), summary ({heading,intro,items:[{label,description}]}), heroImage?, heroImageAlt?. This supplies the single h1.
- Default ArticleTocPlaceholder from ~/components/articles/ArticleTocPlaceholder.
- Named ArticleReferences from ~/components/articles/ArticleReferences, links=[{id,href,title,publisher,category?}]. Use verified research sources, never invented references.
- Default ArticleDisclaimer from ~/components/articles/ArticleDisclaimer.
- Named ArticleImageBlock, ArticleStepList and ArticleResourceCTA from their existing ~/components/articles modules; inspect their props before using them.
- Default ArticleCompanyCTA from ~/components/articles/ArticleCompanyCTA only when the approved editorial action calls for it. Inspect the current props and use the approved offer, not generic invented promises.
- Named ArticleFooterNav from ~/components/articles/ArticleFooterNav (backHref="/articles", topHref="#").

Put the body in a responsive prose container. Every substantial section needs a stable id and data-cf-component-id="section:<id>", data-cf-component-type="section", data-cf-component-label and data-cf-source-section-id for reviewed comments and revisions. Use semantic headings, descriptive links and image alt text. Tables need scoped headers and a horizontally scrollable region so the page itself never overflows a narrow viewport. Keep downloads and images bound to the approved generated media manifests. Do not copy example article facts or public asset URLs into an unrelated article.

Publication also requires a matching app/articles/registry.ts ARTICLE_REGISTRY entry keyed and slugged featured/<slug>, with title,date,description,author,slug,image,imageAlt,hasContent=true, dateModified and the stable analyticsArticleId. Preserve every existing entry. Include matching approved editorial metadata when present. The Vite glob in app/routes/articles.slug.tsx loads the content module automatically; do not add manual imports there. A content file alone is not a registered article. Preserve the listing, exact canonical, real unknown-slug 404 and reviewed integration marker. Build and browser verification must pass before publication.

# ArticleLayout ## Purpose Article-page wrapper for SEO, JSON-LD, breadcrumbs, optional TOC/sidebar, professional carousel, related content, and next-article navigation. Implement in `app/articles/ArticleLayout.tsx`. Define a named `ArticleLayout` export for this component; this does not establish a project-wide export convention. ## Props Use a `type ArticleLayoutProps` alias and a separate `import type { ReactNode } from "react";`. Reuse project domain types; `Event` means the domain event type, not the DOM type. | Prop | Type | Default | Description | |---|---|---|---| | article | ArticleMetadata | Required | Title, description, slug, date, author, etc. | | children | ReactNode | Required | Article content | | showHero | boolean | true | Show hero | | showDate | boolean | true | Show publication date | | showDisclaimer | boolean | false | Show legal disclaimer | | breadcrumb | string | — | Single breadcrumb text | | breadcrumbItems | BreadcrumbItem[] | — | Breadcrumb items | | titleTag | "h1" \| "h2" | "h1" | Title element | | featuredProfessionals | Professional[] | — | Featured professionals | | featuredProfessionalsTitle | string | — | Professionals heading | | featuredProfessionalsPersona | string | — | Persona filter | | faqItems | FAQItem[] | — | Visible FAQs and schema | | howTo | HowToSchema | — | HowTo structured data | | summaryHighlights | string[] | — | Key points | | containerMaxWidthClassName | string | — | Outer max-width override | | contentMaxWidthClassName | string | — | Content max-width override | | containerClassName | string | — | Extra outer classes | | containerInnerClassName | string | — | Extra inner classes | | contentPaddingClassName | string | — | Padding override | | upcomingEvents | Event[] | — | Sidebar events | | showHeader | boolean | true | Show page header | ## Structure and React Router Integration Use as the outermost article-page wrapper: - Optional header, breadcrumbs, and hero. - Main article content with optional TOC/events aside. - Optional FAQ, professionals carousel, and related articles. - Footer with next-article navigation. Use `Link` from `"react-router"` for internal breadcrumbs, related articles, and next links; native anchors for TOC fragments and external URLs. Let the route own SEO metadata through its `meta` export and the document's `Meta` integration. Emit safely serialized JSON-LD scripts, not a nested ``. Do not introduce loaders or actions solely for this layout. ## Styling and Accessibility Use Tailwind: constrained full-width outer container, readable content width, mobile single column, desktop sticky sidebar. Class overrides replace their corresponding defaults. Use semantic `article`, `aside`, and labelled `nav` elements. Avoid nested `main` landmarks. Provide skip links, correct heading hierarchy, image alt text, and keyboard-accessible carousel controls. ## Semantic Hints `layout`, `article`, `wrapper`, `container`, `page-layout`, `article-page`, `article-container`, `prose`, `content-wrapper` ## Example Route `app/articles/ExampleArticle.tsx`; uses the component export specified above. ```tsx import { ArticleLayout } from "./ArticleLayout"; const ARTICLE = { title: "Reading Guide", description: "A practical reading guide.", slug: "reading-guide", date: "2026-01-01", author: "Editorial Team", }; export function meta() { return [ { title: ARTICLE.title }, { name: "description", content: ARTICLE.description }, ]; } export default function ExampleArticle() { return (

 ); } ``` Match `ARTICLE` to the project's actual `ArticleMetadata` shape. No `"use client"` directive is needed unless this module becomes a client-only analytics module.
framework_component_specs.ArticleEnhancer:
# ArticleEnhancer ## Purpose Client-side article wrapper that generates a TOC and injects HowTo/MediaObject JSON-LD. Uses `MutationObserver` for dynamic content. ## Files and conventions - Implement in `app/articles/ArticleEnhancer.tsx`. - Begin with `"use client";`. In React Router this is not a client-only execution boundary; defer browser work to effects. - Use named React imports, `createPortal` from `"react-dom"`, and separate type imports. - Define props with a `type` alias. Use explicit helper parameter/return types, two-space indentation, semicolons, and double quotes. - Component export style is not prescribed. ## Props | Prop | Type | Default | Description | |------|------|---------|-------------| | `articleTitle` | `string` | Required | Article title for structured data | | `contentSelector` | `string` | Required | CSS selector for the content container | | `articleDescription` | `string` | — | Structured-data description | | `enableToc` | `boolean` | `true` | Generate TOC | | `enableHowTo` | `boolean` | `true` | Inject HowTo schema | | `enableMediaObject` | `boolean` | `true` | Inject MediaObject schema for images | | `children` | `ReactNode` | — | Article content to wrap | Import `ReactNode` using `import type { ReactNode } from "react";`. ## Semantic hints `enhancer`, `wrapper`, `article-wrapper`, `enhancement`, `seo`, `structured-data`, `meta` ## Usage Usually owned by `ArticleLayout`; wrap article content and provide an `ArticleTocPlaceholder` portal target. ## Behavior and structure 1. Render children unchanged. Scan `h2`/`h3` within the selected container in `useEffect`. 2. Preserve existing IDs; assign stable, unique IDs where missing. Remove emoji from TOC labels and nest h3 entries beneath their preceding h2. 3. Use `createPortal` to render semantic TOC navigation into `ArticleTocPlaceholder`. Use native fragment links for headings. 4. Detect instructional step lists and generate HowTo JSON-LD using the title and optional description. 5. Generate MediaObject JSON-LD for content images with usable URLs. 6. Insert owned `application/ld+json` scripts into `document.head`; serialize with `JSON.stringify`. 7. Debounce observer callbacks. Avoid self-triggering updates and duplicate scripts. Disconnect observers, clear timers, and remove owned scripts on cleanup. 8. Honor enable flags and rescan when props or React Router location changes. Use `useLocation` from `"react-router"` for navigation awareness. Keep initial rendering SSR-safe: no `window` or `document` access during render. Handle missing containers/portal targets safely. No loaders or actions are required. ## React Router route example `app/routes/ArticleExample.tsx` below assumes a named enhancer export only for this example; match the implementation’s actual export. ```tsx import { ArticleEnhancer } from "../articles/ArticleEnhancer"; export default function ArticleExample() { return (

Step-by-Step Guide

  1. Choose a learning goal.
  2. Practice with a small project.
); } ``` Use `#article-toc-placeholder` as this example’s `ArticleTocPlaceholder` target.

motion.notes: Static captures do not establish transition duration, hover transforms or animated behaviour. Reuse existing interactions; do not infer card lift, marquee motion, parallax, underline animation or button bounce from the visual style.

spacing.grid: Persistent desktop two-part composition: narrow navigation rail plus a broad main column. Directory featured strip: four equal columns, approximately 264px wide by 200px high, 16px gaps. Article opening: two equal approximately 472px columns with a 16px gap beneath a 960px-wide hero. Directory results region combines a compact left calendar with a wider right-hand result stack.
spacing.notes: The article's centered 960px reading layout sits inside the main column, not at the centre of the full browser viewport. Do not let the navigation rail overlap the content or reduce the entire site to a centred 960px column. Mobile screenshots are not supplied; responsive behaviour must follow the existing implementation rather than an invented miniature desktop rail.
spacing.base_unit: An apparent 4px/8px spacing rhythm, supported by measured 12, 16, 20, 24, 32 and 48px values; no explicit custom spacing scale is defined in Tailwind.
spacing.content_width: Article detail: measured 960px. At 1440px desktop, the article spans approximately x=350 to x=1310. The wider main-column shell begins around x=232 and ends around x=1428; the directory's inner content is approximately 1104px wide.
spacing.section_rhythm: Homepage major rounded panels have approximately 24–48px cream gaps. Directory hero is followed by roughly 44px before featured cards, then approximately 48px before 'All Articles'. Article title is followed by a 16px gap before the summary/photo pair. Editorial body components should retain the existing my-12 rhythm where supplied.
spacing.container_padding: Desktop page edge: approximately 12–16px. Left rail: 16px from the viewport edge and approximately 188px wide. Main shell begins at approximately 232px, leaving a 28px rail-to-main gap. Large directory/home panels use approximately 48px internal padding; article-title panel uses approximately 56px. Summary panel uses approximately 32px.

spec.summary: MLAI has a playful, poster-like Australian community identity built from a warm cream canvas, a highly distinctive left-hand navigation rail of numbered, saturated-colour tiles, oversized typography and large rounded panels. Its visual language combines electric orange, violet, royal blue, hot pink, lemon yellow and turquoise with near-black, rather than relying on a conventional white-and-grey technology aesthetic. The homepage uses monumental condensed display lettering; the articles directory uses a bold sans-serif headline on a yellow panel; article detail pages switch to a large, genuinely underlined Georgia headline on turquoise. Content alternates between open cream space and strongly coloured, inset rounded containers. A sunglasses-wearing kangaroo supplies the irreverent brand signature, while article photography remains natural and human. The overall result is confident, practical, energetic and community-led, with thin outlines and minimal shadows rather than heavy neo-brutalist drop shadows.
do_rules: Keep the warm #F5F0E6 canvas visible around and between content regions.
Preserve the desktop left rail with the kangaroo image and seven numbered, individually coloured navigation tiles.
Use the correct typography for each page type: condensed display on the homepage, bold Inter for the directory, and underlined Georgia for article detail.
Use large, flat, saturated panels with generous internal padding and context-specific radii.
Keep article detail at approximately 960px within the main column, with a turquoise title panel and the established orange-summary/photo opening when using the captured template.
Give the directory a yellow hero, integrated search/topic controls and a four-colour featured strip before the calendar-indexed results.
Use the measured orange #FF3D00 and violet #4B0DB3 rather than generic Tailwind approximations when defining brand fills.
Use white utility surfaces and muted metadata sparingly, subordinate to cream and the bright brand palette.
Keep borders fine and shadows restrained; reserve the strong dark inset outline for the appropriate active/emphatic component.
Reuse the existing article components, shell, footer, route contracts and assets instead of building a parallel design system.
Treat screenshot-derived turquoise, blue, pink and lemon hex values as approximations until verified against the actual source tokens.
Keep new content accessible, with meaningful image alternatives, proper headings, labelled controls and usable keyboard interactions.
dont_rules: Do not replace the left rail with a conventional horizontal SaaS navbar.
Do not turn the site into a generic white/slate blog with small blue accents.
Do not apply the homepage's 403.2px numeral size or -10.08px tracking to article titles.
Do not use Georgia for every heading or Inter for the captured article h1.
Do not invent a coloured underline swash, marker highlight or decorative terminal dot.
Do not misrepresent category chips as a universal filled-pill eyebrow system.
Do not add thick black borders and offset hard shadows to every card or button.
Do not make all major sections full-width background bands separated by full-bleed rules.
Do not invent stock vector robots, abstract AI brains, glassmorphism or gradient mesh backgrounds.
Do not duplicate the h1, breadcrumb or author area already supplied by the existing article layout.
Do not infer a fixed or sticky rail solely from repeated screenshot placement.
Do not fabricate article cards, dates, author information, pagination counts or downloads when the directory is empty.
Do not treat the consolidated h2=14px and h3=12px readings as the entire site's visual heading hierarchy.
Do not invent hover or accordion behaviour that has not been verified in the current components.

navigation.logo: A cropped, realistic/composited kangaroo head wearing pixelated dark sunglasses on a flat turquoise rounded rectangle. Retain the existing 'MLAI Kangaroo logo' asset. A plain MLAI wordmark appears at the lower-left of the homepage hero; a much larger orange MLAI display wordmark appears in the about section.
navigation.notes: The rail repeats across all three page types. The measured nav_height=750px refers to a large navigation region, not a conventional 750px horizontal header. Sticky/fixed scrolling behaviour is not demonstrated by a static image; retain the supplied false sticky token unless the existing component establishes otherwise.
navigation.footer: Measured background is black, with an approximate captured height of 633px. Exact footer column structure and visible typography are not established by the supplied visible crop. Reuse the existing footer rather than inventing a generic multi-column footer. The near-black computed footer text token should not be treated as proof that visible footer copy is black on black.
navigation.header: The defining desktop navigation is a left rail, not a horizontal masthead. At 1440px, it sits at x=16 with approximately 188px width. A turquoise kangaroo image tile at the top is about 188×94px with 14–16px corners. After roughly 24px, seven vertically stacked navigation tiles are approximately 100px tall with 8px gaps. Each tile places its small number at the upper-left and its 20px label near the lower-left. The main content starts around x=232. Homepage utility actions are placed inside the large hero panel, not across a separate top navigation bar.
navigation.nav_links: Exact visible sequence and colour association: 1 Hello — orange; 2 Events — violet; 3 Founder Tools — near-black; 4 People — royal blue; 5 Studio — hot pink; 6 Articles — bright yellow; 7 Hackathons — turquoise. Labels are white on the first five dark/saturated tiles and black on yellow/turquoise. The active Hello tile in the homepage capture has a dark inset outline.
navigation.cta_in_nav: No CTA is embedded among the seven numbered destination tiles. The homepage hero's top row contains Log in at left in turquoise, Donate near the centre in orange, and See Events at right in black, each with an icon. Do not add that utility row above article detail unless the existing shell does so.

typography.notes: Typography deliberately changes register by context: condensed campaign display on the homepage, bold Inter on the directory and Georgia on article detail. Preserve this contrast. The article title spans two generous lines in the supplied desktop capture; it is not a compact sans-serif blog header.

scale.h1: Article detail: 60px Georgia, weight 700, approximately 1.25 line-height, black, underlined. Directory: approximately 60px Inter, weight 700, tight approximately 1.0 line-height, near-black.
scale.h2: Visible directory section heading 'All Articles': approximately 24px, bold sans-serif. Large homepage section headings such as 'Upcoming Events' are approximately 60px at the original desktop scale. The consolidated 14px h2 reading describes a small semantic heading somewhere in the DOM, not the site's universal visual h2 scale.
scale.body: 16px / 24px Inter, weight 400; compact supporting text and answer copy can be 14px / 20px.
scale.eyebrow: Article key-facts heading: approximately 14px / 20px, weight 700, uppercase, modest tracking. Topic chips: measured 13px, weight 600. Breadcrumbs: approximately 14px.

typography.accents: The article title is decorated with an actual thin black text underline that follows each wrapped line. The directory title ends with an ordinary black period. Homepage editorial 'We Are' uses oversized italic serif type. No marker swipe, coloured terminal dot or hand-drawn underline swash is established.
typography.hero_size: Homepage numeral: measured 403.2px at the sampled rendering, with responsive viewport scaling. Directory and article title: 60px. Do not apply the 403.2px numeral scale to editorial titles.
typography.body_weight: 400; 600 for chips, some utility actions and emphasized labels.
typography.hero_weight: 700 measured for the homepage hero; visually extremely dense because of the condensed display face. Directory and article title also use 700.
typography.line_height: Body: 24px at 16px. Directory headline: approximately 60px at 60px. Article title: approximately 75px at 60px. Featured titles: approximately 31px at 24px. Compact summary answers: approximately 20px at 14px.
typography.display_font: The homepage uses a very heavy condensed sans-serif display face for '1000' and 'AUSTRALIAN STARTUPS'. Its exact family is not established by the supplied tokens; reuse the existing display-face declaration rather than substituting Georgia or ordinary Inter.
typography.heading_font: Georgia for the article-detail title and editorial serif moments; Inter for directory headings, cards, navigation and most utility headings.
typography.heading_weight: 700 as the primary heading weight; 900 is present in the wider font-weight set but is not a universal heading requirement.
typography.letter_spacing: Homepage display numeral: -10.08px measured. Directory headline is visibly tight; preserve the existing heading classes rather than applying the numeral's spacing. Body and navigation use normal tracking. The key-facts label has slight positive tracking.
typography.text_transform: Most titles and navigation labels are sentence/title case. 'AUSTRALIAN STARTUPS', article key-facts labels and date metadata use uppercase. Do not uppercase all editorial headings.

card.name: Flat saturated feature tile and quiet utility card
card.notes: Do not render every article as an identical white thumbnail card. The coloured featured strip and the date-driven result area are different layers of the directory.
card.classes: feature: rounded-2xl p-6 text-white border-0 shadow-none; utility: rounded-3xl border bg-white/70 p-8 shadow-sm
card.description: The directory's featured articles use four flat orange, violet, near-black and royal-blue tiles, approximately 264×200px with 16px radius, 24px padding and bold 24px white titles aligned toward the lower portion. The first tile includes a cropped human photograph heavily integrated into the orange treatment. Utility results instead use white or translucent-white surfaces with pale 1px borders and subtle shadows, inside a larger rounded directory container.

cards_lists.notes: Card geometry is deliberately varied by purpose: big 40px-radius panels, medium 24px utility containers, 16px content tiles and full pills. Preserve hierarchy rather than flattening everything to one radius and one card style.

list_item.name: Calendar-indexed article result / outlined event row
list_item.notes: The article key-facts panel uses a simpler black-bullet question-and-answer list directly on orange, not nested cards.
list_item.classes: event: rounded-2xl border border-white/20 p-5; result: rounded-2xl border border-gray-200 bg-white
list_item.description: Directory results are stacked white rounded items beside a calendar, with small uppercase muted date metadata, a dark article title and a right-aligned circular pale navigation control. Homepage event rows are transparent on violet, outlined in white at 20% opacity, radius 16px, padding 20px; they place an orange date block at left, title and location in the middle, and an orange Register button at right.

badge_pill.name: Small topic chip
badge_pill.notes: These chips are filters/topics, not the universal section-eyebrow style. Do not add category pills above every heading.
badge_pill.classes: inline-flex items-center rounded-full px-[14px] py-[6px] text-[13px] font-semibold
badge_pill.description: Compact fully rounded filled pills. Measured orange and violet versions use white 13px/600 labels with 6px 14px padding. In the directory search, AI is orange, ML violet, Community dark grey, and Australia yellow with dark text. Larger translucent rounded badges also occur elsewhere in the measured DOM.

image_style.notes: Use meaningful alternatives and existing assets. Do not replace the kangaroo with a generic AI glyph. Avoid default landscape thumbnails when matching the visible tall article image. Visible pixels take precedence over an alt string when identifying the captured image's composition.

spec.tone_of_voice: Plain-English Australian community communication: practical, welcoming, direct and confident without enterprise jargon.
