active_design_snapshot.design_spec_md:
# Website Design Spec

MLAI has a playful, poster-like Australian community identity built from a warm cream canvas, a highly distinctive left-hand navigation rail of numbered, saturated-colour tiles, oversized typography and large rounded panels. Its visual language combines electric orange, violet, royal blue, hot pink, lemon yellow and turquoise with near-black, rather than relying on a conventional white-and-grey technology aesthetic. The homepage uses monumental condensed display lettering; the articles directory uses a bold sans-serif headline on a yellow panel; article detail pages switch to a large, genuinely underlined Georgia headline on turquoise. Content alternates between open cream space and strongly coloured, inset rounded containers. A sunglasses-wearing kangaroo supplies the irreverent brand signature, while article photography remains natural and human. The overall result is confident, practical, energetic and community-led, with thin outlines and minimal shadows rather than heavy neo-brutalist drop shadows.

## Color system
- Background: #F5F0E6 / rgb(245, 240, 230): the visible page canvas across the homepage, directory and article detail, including the space behind the left navigation.
- Text: #1A1A1A for the principal brand typography; #000000 also appears in article headings and text. The generic computed body token is oklch(0.145 0 0).  ·  Muted: Muted utility text uses the measured cool-neutral family, including oklch(0.373 0.034 259.733); lighter dates, counts and placeholders appear approximately #6B7280 to #9CA3AF. These are secondary utility colours, not the dominant brand palette.
- Primary/accent: #FF3D00 / rgb(255, 61, 0): signature orange for Hello navigation, Donate, sponsor panels, event dates, registration buttons, featured content and article key-facts panels. / A multi-accent system: violet #4B0DB3, electric royal blue, hot pink, lemon yellow and turquoise. Each colour identifies a navigation destination or a large content region; orange is not the only accent.
- Border: #1A1A1A for selected or emphatic 2–3px outlines; oklch(0.707 0.022 261.325) for fine section outlines; oklch(0.92 0.004 286.32) for pale utility-card borders; rgba(255,255,255,0.2) on dark coloured event rows.
- Ratios: Composition-dependent rather than a single global ratio. On the homepage opening, cream and near-black dominate roughly 80–90% of the main panel, while the rail and small CTAs supply concentrated colour. The directory opening allocates approximately its upper 370px to a large lemon panel, followed by substantial cream space and four saturated featured tiles. The article opening places a turquoise title panel above an orange summary and a large photograph. Within each region, use one decisive flat colour; do not distribute all brand colours evenly across every paragraph, badge or control.

## Typography
- Heading/display: Georgia for the article-detail title and editorial serif moments; Inter for directory headings, cards, navigation and most utility headings. / The homepage uses a very heavy condensed sans-serif display face for '1000' and 'AUSTRALIAN STARTUPS'. Its exact family is not established by the supplied tokens; reuse the existing display-face declaration rather than substituting Georgia or ordinary Inter.
- Body: Inter, with a sans-serif fallback. (400; 600 for chips, some utility actions and emphasized labels., Body: 24px at 16px. Directory headline: approximately 60px at 60px. Article title: approximately 75px at 60px. Featured titles: approximately 31px at 24px. Compact summary answers: approximately 20px at 14px.)
- Hero: Homepage numeral: measured 403.2px at the sampled rendering, with responsive viewport scaling. Directory and article title: 60px. Do not apply the 403.2px numeral scale to editorial titles. / 700 measured for the homepage hero; visually extremely dense because of the condensed display face. Directory and article title also use 700.
- Accents: The article title is decorated with an actual thin black text underline that follows each wrapped line. The directory title ends with an ordinary black period. Homepage editorial 'We Are' uses oversized italic serif type. No marker swipe, coloured terminal dot or hand-drawn underline swash is established.
- Transform: Most titles and navigation labels are sentence/title case. 'AUSTRALIAN STARTUPS', article key-facts labels and date metadata use uppercase. Do not uppercase all editorial headings.  ·  Tracking: Homepage display numeral: -10.08px measured. Directory headline is visibly tight; preserve the existing heading classes rather than applying the numeral's spacing. Body and navigation use normal tracking. The key-facts label has slight positive tracking.

## Spacing & layout
- Content width: Article detail: measured 960px. At 1440px desktop, the article spans approximately x=350 to x=1310. The wider main-column shell begins around x=232 and ends around x=1428; the directory's inner content is approximately 1104px wide.
- Section rhythm: Homepage major rounded panels have approximately 24–48px cream gaps. Directory hero is followed by roughly 44px before featured cards, then approximately 48px before 'All Articles'. Article title is followed by a 16px gap before the summary/photo pair. Editorial body components should retain the existing my-12 rhythm where supplied.
- Grid: Persistent desktop two-part composition: narrow navigation rail plus a broad main column. Directory featured strip: four equal columns, approximately 264px wide by 200px high, 16px gaps. Article opening: two equal approximately 472px columns with a 16px gap beneath a 960px-wide hero. Directory results region combines a compact left calendar with a wider right-hand result stack.

## Borders & shadows
- Border: 1px for large outlined cream sections and utility cards; 2px for measured cream buttons; approximately 3px inset outline for the active orange navigation tile. Ink #1A1A1A for emphatic outlines; measured oklch(0.707 0.022 261.325) for subtle large-panel outlines; very pale neutral for directory cards; white at 20% opacity for cards on violet.
- Radius: Rounded, but not uniformly pill-shaped: approximately 14–16px on navigation and featured cards, 16px on article hero and summary, 24px on directory result containers, 40px on large homepage and directory panels, and 9999px on small pill controls.
- Shadow: Predominantly none. Measured utility shadow: 0 1px 3px 0 rgba(0,0,0,0.1), 0 1px 2px -1px rgba(0,0,0,0.1). Measured cream-button shadow: 0 4px 6px -1px rgba(0,0,0,0.1), 0 2px 4px -2px rgba(0,0,0,0.1). Active navigation uses a 0 0 0 3px inset #1A1A1A ring, not an offset shadow.

## Buttons
- Primary: bg-[#FF3D00] text-white rounded-full border-0 shadow-none px-[14px] py-[6px] text-[13px] font-semibold
- Secondary: bg-[#F5F0E6] text-[#1A1A1A] border-2 border-[#1A1A1A] rounded-[14px] p-3 font-normal shadow-md
- Links: Ordinary links inherit dark body text unless their component reverses them. Breadcrumbs are dark, compact and slash-separated, with an outlined home icon. Article-title underlining is a defining editorial decoration, not evidence that every navigation link is underlined. Featured article tiles behave as large linked surfaces.

## Cards, lists & badges
- Card: feature: rounded-2xl p-6 text-white border-0 shadow-none; utility: rounded-3xl border bg-white/70 p-8 shadow-sm
- Badge/pill: inline-flex items-center rounded-full px-[14px] py-[6px] text-[13px] font-semibold

## Navigation & chrome
- Header: The defining desktop navigation is a left rail, not a horizontal masthead. At 1440px, it sits at x=16 with approximately 188px width. A turquoise kangaroo image tile at the top is about 188×94px with 14–16px corners. After roughly 24px, seven vertically stacked navigation tiles are approximately 100px tall with 8px gaps. Each tile places its small number at the upper-left and its 20px label near the lower-left. The main content starts around x=232. Homepage utility actions are placed inside the large hero panel, not across a separate top navigation bar.
- Logo: A cropped, realistic/composited kangaroo head wearing pixelated dark sunglasses on a flat turquoise rounded rectangle. Retain the existing 'MLAI Kangaroo logo' asset. A plain MLAI wordmark appears at the lower-left of the homepage hero; a much larger orange MLAI display wordmark appears in the about section.
- In-nav CTA: No CTA is embedded among the seven numbered destination tiles. The homepage hero's top row contains Log in at left in turquoise, Donate near the centre in orange, and See Events at right in black, each with an icon. Do not add that utility row above article detail unless the existing shell does so.
- Footer: Measured background is black, with an approximate captured height of 633px. Exact footer column structure and visible typography are not established by the supplied visible crop. Reuse the existing footer rather than inventing a generic multi-column footer. The near-black computed footer text token should not be treated as proof that visible footer copy is black on black.

## Imagery & illustration
- Photography: Human, approachable editorial photography rather than futuristic AI renders. The visible article opening uses a large natural-light portrait of a woman in a dark sweater, cropped vertically in the right-hand column. Image metadata also references a practical laptop/checklist/coffee scene. Choose imagery around real work, people and everyday business tasks.
- Illustration: The brand mascot is the sunglasses-wearing kangaroo, using realistic photographic/composited texture against a flat turquoise field. There is no evidence for a flat-vector mascot system, robot illustrations or abstract 3D AI artwork.
- Icons: Small, simple outline interface icons: home, search, login, heart, chevrons and location pin. Most are single-colour with clean, modest strokes; white icons reverse out on black or violet where appropriate.

## Layout grammar
- Section pattern: A continuous warm-cream page supports large inset rounded panels; this is not a sequence of full-bleed, edge-to-edge horizontal bands. On the homepage, a thin-outlined cream hero is followed by an orange sponsor panel, a thin-outlined cream about panel and a violet events panel. The directory starts with a broad yellow rounded hero, then returns to cream for a four-card featured strip and the All Articles/calendar area. Article detail is narrower: turquoise title panel, then a two-column orange-summary/photo composition, followed by editorial content using existing article components.
- Band backgrounds: Outer continuous canvas: #F5F0E6., Homepage hero/about panel: #F5F0E6 with fine neutral outline., Sponsor region: #FF3D00., Events region: #4B0DB3., Directory hero: vivid electric lemon, approximately #FFFF25., Article title panel: turquoise, approximately #00E8CF., Article key-facts panel: #FF3D00., Directory utility surfaces: white or translucent white., Footer: #000000.
- Section divider: Cream gutters separate the major rounded panels. Homepage outlined panels can contain fine horizontal rules inset to their content width. Small coloured horizontal strokes appear near the right edge in the gaps before major homepage sections. There is no evidence of a universal full-bleed hairline divider between every section.
- Eyebrow: breadcrumb: text-sm font-normal; key-facts: text-sm font-bold uppercase; section-index: text-sm
- Heading accent: Article detail uses a continuous black typographic underline beneath each wrapped line of its Georgia h1. The directory headline is undecorated bold black sans-serif with a normal terminal period. Homepage 'We Are' is oversized italic serif; the large MLAI wordmark and parenthetical expansion are orange. Do not add a marker swash or a coloured terminal period.
- FAQ pattern: The visible opening summary presents bold questions and smaller answers in a black-bullet list directly on the orange panel, with no separate question cards. A dedicated lower-page FAQ/accordion construction is not established by the visible evidence. Reuse ArticleFAQ for actual FAQ sections rather than inventing bordered cards, chevrons or divider behaviour.
- Card metaphor: The site is panel-led, not uniformly card-led. Large coloured or outlined containers establish major moments; ordinary headings and explanatory copy also live directly on cream. The directory introduces distinct feature tiles and quieter calendar-indexed result cards. Article key facts share one orange panel rather than becoming many nested cards.

## Tone of voice
Plain-English Australian community communication: practical, welcoming, direct and confident without enterprise jargon. The brand speaks to builders, learners and founders, with a volunteer/not-for-profit emphasis. Short energetic phrases such as 'Let's get on it' coexist with careful task-oriented guidance. Article copy should use specific examples, realistic next steps, researched claims and labelled uncertainty rather than inflated promises about AI.

## Do / Don't
- DO: Keep the warm #F5F0E6 canvas visible around and between content regions.
- DO: Preserve the desktop left rail with the kangaroo image and seven numbered, individually coloured navigation tiles.
- DO: Use the correct typography for each page type: condensed display on the homepage, bold Inter for the directory, and underlined Georgia for article detail.
- DO: Use large, flat, saturated panels with generous internal padding and context-specific radii.
- DO: Keep article detail at approximately 960px within the main column, with a turquoise title panel and the established orange-summary/photo opening when using the captured template.
- DO: Give the directory a yellow hero, integrated search/topic controls and a four-colour featured strip before the calendar-indexed results.
- DO: Use the measured orange #FF3D00 and violet #4B0DB3 rather than generic Tailwind approximations when defining brand fills.
- DO: Use white utility surfaces and muted metadata sparingly, subordinate to cream and the bright brand palette.
- DO: Keep borders fine and shadows restrained; reserve the strong dark inset outline for the appropriate active/emphatic component.
- DO: Reuse the existing article components, shell, footer, route contracts and assets instead of building a parallel design system.
- DO: Treat screenshot-derived turquoise, blue, pink and lemon hex values as approximations until verified against the actual source tokens.
- DO: Keep new content accessible, with meaningful image alternatives, proper headings, labelled controls and usable keyboard interactions.
- DON'T: Do not replace the left rail with a conventional horizontal SaaS navbar.
- DON'T: Do not turn the site into a generic white/slate blog with small blue accents.
- DON'T: Do not apply the homepage's 403.2px numeral size or -10.08px tracking to article titles.
- DON'T: Do not use Georgia for every heading or Inter for the captured article h1.
- DON'T: Do not invent a coloured underline swash, marker highlight or decorative terminal dot.
- DON'T: Do not misrepresent category chips as a universal filled-pill eyebrow system.
- DON'T: Do not add thick black borders and offset hard shadows to every card or button.
- DON'T: Do not make all major sections full-width background bands separated by full-bleed rules.
- DON'T: Do not invent stock vector robots, abstract AI brains, glassmorphism or gradient mesh backgrounds.
- DON'T: Do not duplicate the h1, breadcrumb or author area already supplied by the existing article layout.
- DON'T: Do not infer a fixed or sticky rail solely from repeated screenshot placement.
- DON'T: Do not fabricate article cards, dates, author information, pagination counts or downloads when the directory is empty.
- DON'T: Do not treat the consolidated h2=14px and h3=12px readings as the entire site's visual heading hierarchy.
- DON'T: Do not invent hover or accordion behaviour that has not been verified in the current components.

## Article application rules
- Page shell: Retain the shared cream canvas and left navigation rail. Centre the existing 960px article container inside the main content region; at the supplied 1440px desktop size its left edge is approximately 350px, not the directory's 280px inner edge. Keep the opening approximately 24px below the viewport top. Reuse the current article layout and footer.
- Hero: Use the existing ArticleHeroHeader and its actual props. Match the visible turquoise rounded rectangle, approximately 960px wide and 338px tall for the captured title, 16px radius and around 56px padding. Breadcrumbs sit above the single black Georgia h1. The h1 is approximately 60px/75px, weight 700, genuinely underlined and wraps naturally. Do not insert an extra eyebrow, duplicate title or unrelated hero CTA.
- Headings: Preserve one h1 owned by ArticleHeroHeader when present. Use the existing article component/prose styles for h2 and h3 rather than propagating the serif hero treatment everywhere. The key-facts heading is a small bold uppercase label, not an h2-sized display statement. Keep anchor IDs and heading hierarchy stable.
- Body: Use Inter 16px/24px with readable dark text and the existing text-gray-900/text-gray-700 conventions where implemented. Preserve my-12 component spacing. Practical answers inside the summary can use 14px/20px supporting text under stronger 16px questions. Keep wide tables in horizontally scrollable regions. Do not stretch long-form paragraphs across the entire main shell merely because the homepage is wide.
- Cards: For the captured opening template, place one orange key-facts panel beside one equally wide, rounded, edge-to-edge photograph, separated by 16px. The orange panel has approximately 32px padding, dark text and simple black bullet-led questions with answers. Subsequent callouts should use the existing ArticleCallout component and its info, success, warning or brand variant; do not hand-build a competing nested-card language.
- Buttons: Use existing approved resource and company CTA components. Brand actions can use the compact rounded orange/violet treatment, while secondary actions may use the measured cream outlined button. Do not add a large sales CTA to every section. ArticleCompanyCTA requires title, body, buttonText and buttonHref, with a verified destination.
- Badges: Use compact topic chips only when the current article layout or approved brief calls for them. Do not add a chip row above the turquoise title merely to echo the directory search. Keep breadcrumb navigation as bare dark text and icons.
- Empty state: An article detail route should not invent an empty article or dummy metadata. Missing/unpublished content should follow the repository's real 404 or unavailable-content contract. If an optional related-content region has no items, omit the empty grid or show a short plain message within the existing section styling; do not create fake cards.
- Must use: Shared cream canvas and existing navigation shell.
- Must use: Existing ArticleHeroHeader when that is the neighbouring article contract.
- Must use: A single article h1 with the captured turquoise/underlined-Georgia treatment.
- Must use: Existing article component exports and verified props.
- Must use: ArticleFAQ for dedicated FAQs, with question/answer items and only supported optional props.
- Must use: Meaningful image alternatives and approved asset URLs.
- Must use: Stable existing metadata, canonical ownership, anchors and resource links.
- Must avoid: A generic white blog masthead replacing the turquoise hero.
- Must avoid: Duplicate breadcrumbs, titles or author blocks.
- Must avoid: A hand-invented FAQ accordion appearance.
- Must avoid: Missing ArticleResourceDownload or ArticleSummaryCard imports.
- Must avoid: Unapproved service chips, downloads, company promotion or warning banners.
- Must avoid: Next.js routing APIs or a parallel article scaffold.

## Directory application rules
- Page shell: Keep the shared left navigation and cream canvas. The main yellow hero starts approximately x=232, y=12 at 1440px, spans about 1196px and uses around 40px radius. Below it, use an inner content region beginning around x=278–280 with about 1104px width. Do not use the narrower 960px article-detail container for the entire directory.
- Hero: Use the broad electric-lemon rounded panel with approximately 48px padding. The headline is black Inter, approximately 60px/60px, weight 700, arranged into two lines at the captured width: a strong editorial statement about writing on AI, machine learning and community. Follow with a 16px/24px plain-English description and a white search container approximately 700×58px. Keep search and the small AI, ML, Community and Australia topic pills together inside that white control area.
- Headings: Directory h1 is bold sans-serif, not underlined Georgia. Keep its ordinary terminal punctuation and no added eyebrow. 'All Articles' is a much smaller approximately 24px bold heading, followed by a muted 14px result-count line. Featured titles are approximately 24px/31px white bold text.
- Body: Use dark 16px/24px explanatory text on yellow and cream, with muted utility counts and dates. Preserve generous separation between the hero, featured strip and all-articles section. The listing area is not a uniform wall of blog cards: retain the calendar/date navigation beside the result stack where the current directory provides it.
- Cards: Place four equal featured tiles in a single desktop row, approximately 264×200px, 16px gaps, 16px corners and 24px padding. Use orange, violet, near-black and royal blue in that order for the captured treatment; one tile may integrate tinted photography. Below, use the pale rounded outer results container, a compact calendar column and white bordered article rows with dates and circular arrow affordances.
- Buttons: Keep topic filters compact, fully rounded and colour-coded. Use small, quiet previous/next calendar controls rather than large boxed buttons. Search must remain a usable input, not a decorative hero element. Any empty-state action should reuse an existing compact pill or plain link and point to a verified destination.
- Badges: Use the existing small AI orange, ML violet, Community dark-grey and Australia yellow topic pills inside the search region. Their category/filter role should remain explicit. Avoid adding oversized tags to every featured card if the existing tile does not show them.
- Empty state: Retain the complete left rail, lemon directory hero, headline, introduction and search region even when there are no articles. Replace the featured strip with nothing rather than fabricated cards. Keep the 'All Articles' heading and show a truthful '0 articles' count. In the normal pale results area, use a restrained message such as 'No articles yet' with one short sentence about future community guides. Do not introduce a new illustration, giant empty-state icon, new accent colour or oversized CTA. For a filtered zero-result state, distinguish 'No articles found' and offer a small clear-filters action only if filtering is implemented. This is an on-brand extension of the observed system, not a claim that the captured site was empty.
- Must use: Shared numbered colour navigation rail and kangaroo logo.
- Must use: Electric-lemon rounded directory hero.
- Must use: Large bold Inter directory headline rather than the article's serif h1.
- Must use: White integrated search/topic control.
- Must use: Four-colour featured strip when real featured articles exist.
- Must use: Clear All Articles heading and truthful count.
- Must use: Existing calendar/results composition when supported by the directory implementation.
- Must use: Cream whitespace and restrained pale utility containers.
- Must avoid: A plain white header followed by a generic three-column thumbnail grid.
- Must avoid: Using the article-detail turquoise/Georgia title panel for the directory.
- Must avoid: Invented featured articles, placeholder dates or fake result totals.
- Must avoid: A filled eyebrow pill above the directory headline.
- Must avoid: An empty directory that drops all brand colour and shell elements.
- Must avoid: Large decorative empty-state artwork that competes with the existing kangaroo identity.

## Required motifs (review must enforce)
- Warm #F5F0E6 outer canvas rather than a generic white/slate shell.
- The seven numbered, colour-coded desktop navigation tiles beneath the sunglasses-kangaroo logo.
- Large inset rounded panels with decisive flat brand colours and generous spacing.
- Correct page-specific hero typography: bold Inter on lemon for the directory; underlined black Georgia on turquoise for article detail.
- Orange as a recurring brand anchor, including featured content or the article key-facts region where appropriate.
- Restrained thin outlines and soft utility shadows, not universal hard offset shadows.
- Distinct directory feature tiles and calendar/result region rather than interchangeable generic blog cards.

spec.title: Use an Artificial Intelligence Design Assistant to Prototype
spec.meta_title: Artificial intelligence design assistant for prototypes
spec.meta_description: Prototype a hypothetical small-business workflow with synthetic data, check its interactions and plan a capped pilot before paying for development.

summary_items.label: What can an artificial intelligence design assistant produce?
summary_items.description: Some AI design tools generate editable interface layouts from text prompts and provide text-generation features for interface copy. Check whether buttons actually connect screens before treating the output as a clickable prototype.

summary_items.label: How can you prototype a small-business idea?
summary_items.description: For a hypothetical garden-tidy offering, connect three screens: job details, review and edit, and a simulated acknowledgement. Use synthetic data and manually check navigation, error states and mobile readability.

summary_items.label: What should a prototype pilot measure?
summary_items.description: Measure task time, completeness, errors and spending against a comparable baseline. Record customer effort, owner review and setup separately, with time and spending caps and agreed continue, revise or stop thresholds.

sections.heading: Start with one customer task, not a whole product
paragraphs: For a hypothetical first prototype, give an artificial intelligence design assistant one customer task and ask for three connected screens using fictional data. Inspect the generated copy and interactions yourself, then define a small, capped pilot before buying tools or commissioning development. Start with the business problem rather than the software, consistent with business.gov.au’s guidance on introducing AI.

Here, a design assistant means an AI tool you instruct to draft interface layouts, wording or screen specifications. Our hypothetical example is an Australian garden-maintenance business considering a quote-request option for one-off garden tidy-ups. No customer research, prototype testing or validation has been conducted for this example.

AI can help design that flow without being part of the eventual service. A person could still assess every quote request, and the finished form might not need AI at all. A clickable prototype does not establish readiness for live use, secure data handling, functioning integrations or customer demand.

sections.heading: Choose one problem and draw its boundaries
paragraphs: Business.gov.au recommends identifying the business problem first and looking at software you already use when considering solutions. Use this sentence to narrow your idea: “[Customer] needs to [complete task] so that [specific outcome]; we will explore whether [proposed change] helps.” The outcome should be something a person can review, rather than a promise that the tool will deliver a business result.

For the hypothetical garden-maintenance business: “A prospective garden-tidy customer needs to provide enough job information for a person to assess a quote request; we will explore whether a guided request form helps.” Assume the current alternative is a phone or email enquiry. Keep the proposed offering to a request for a one-off garden tidy-up, with a person deciding what happens next.

In this hypothetical exercise, limit the demonstration to three primary screens: enter job details, review and edit those details, then view a clearly labelled simulated acknowledgement. Leave out payments, accounts, live availability, automatic prices and connections to customer-management systems. The final screen should say “Demo only—nothing has been sent” to make its simulated status explicit. During the rehearsal, ask participants what that message means and record any misunderstanding about whether a request or booking was made.

Before generating anything, check whether an existing business-approved tool supports editable screens, linked buttons and a preview. Confirm its current access, sharing, export and pricing restrictions rather than assuming these features are included. Record tool limitations before deciding whether another subscription is needed.

sections.heading: Generate the screens and connect the flow
paragraphs: Give the assistant the customer task, the information it can use, the output you want and the limits it must respect. OpenAI Academy’s small-business workshop calls these Goal, Context, Output and Boundary. They help you explain the request without needing technical language. The hypothetical garden-tidy exercise below applies that structure; it does not assume your chosen tool can generate working, clickable screens.

Check what the assistant actually returns. A screen specification describes the layout, words and behaviour. A static image shows an appearance but has no working controls. A clickable prototype connects screens so someone can follow a route. If the assistant supplies only copy, layouts, specifications or images, use them to assemble editable screens in an already-approved design or presentation tool.

subsections.heading: Copy and adapt this prompt
paragraphs: Replace the bracketed descriptions with your intended business, customer and task. The supplied sample details belong to the hypothetical garden-tidy example and are synthetic, not customer records.

Act as a design assistant for [small business and proposed offering]. Intended user: [customer]. Task: [one customer task]. For this hypothetical exercise, create a low-fidelity, mobile-first prototype with exactly three primary screens: (1) enter the necessary details, (2) review them and edit, and (3) view a simulated acknowledgement. Keep the layout simple and suitable for a narrow phone screen.

For this hypothetical garden-tidy example, use only these synthetic details: Sample Customer A; demo@example.com; service: one-off garden tidy; garden size: small; job note: weed beds and sweep paths. Include labelled fields, concise plain-English copy, a missing-required-field state and an invalid-email state within the relevant screen. Specify forward, edit/back and restart interactions. Use readable text and errors that do not rely on colour alone.

Do not create real accounts, send messages, store submissions, connect services, quote prices or promise availability. Label the final screen: Demo only—nothing has been sent. Output editable screens and an interaction map if supported; otherwise provide a screen specification and exact linking instructions. List assumptions, simulated behaviours and anything requiring human review. Do not invent customer findings.

subsections.heading: Connect the screens and check the preview
paragraphs: For the hypothetical garden-tidy flow, link the job-details screen to the review screen. From review, provide an edit action that returns to job details and a simulated submission action that opens the acknowledgement. Let the acknowledgement restart the demonstration. If the tool has not created those links, connect the buttons manually where supported, then follow each route in preview or presentation mode.
Links alone do not prove that form behaviour works. If the prototype cannot accept typed details, label that behaviour as simulated and record the limitation.

sections.heading: Walk through the prototype before showing it to anyone
paragraphs: Inspect the generated screens yourself rather than accepting the assistant’s claim that they work. Business.gov.au advises checking AI-generated information before relying on it. For this hypothetical garden-tidy prototype, start with the normal route using the supplied synthetic details: enter the request, review it and open the simulated acknowledgement. Check that necessary details are requested before review, the review matches the input and every button reaches its intended destination.

Then try the correction routes. Leave a required field blank, enter an invalid fictional email address, return from review to change the garden size, then restart the demonstration. Keep a short issue log recording the route, expected behaviour, observed behaviour and anything you simulated manually. A drawn error message does not demonstrate functioning validation. If the prototype cannot preserve edited values or respond to invalid input, record that limitation rather than treating the route as passed.

Read the copy alongside those interactions. Look for unexplained fields, missing instructions and promises about prices, availability or messages being sent that the demonstration cannot fulfil. Where “Continue” leaves the destination unclear, use a label such as “Review job details”. Check that the acknowledgement describes a simulation, not a real quote request or booking, and that returning to edit is easy to find.

Open a narrow mobile preview and inspect it for clipped content, readable text and enough spacing to distinguish adjacent buttons. Where the tool permits, try keyboard navigation and zoom, and check whether keyboard focus remains visible. Inspect field labels and make sure errors explain the problem in words rather than relying on colour alone. Mark checks the tool cannot support as “not testable here”. These are practical checks for this exercise, not a comprehensive accessibility audit, security assessment or proof of operational reliability.

Ask for a bounded revision, then repeat the affected route. For example, in this hypothetical prototype: “On the review screen, add an Edit job details action that returns to the entry screen; keep all other copy unchanged.” Check the revised copy and links yourself, and update the issue log with what changed, what remains unresolved and what is still simulated.

sections.heading: Draft a capped pilot before committing money
paragraphs: Plan a usability rehearsal with synthetic information, not a live quote-request service. For the hypothetical garden-tidy offering, invite willing participants who resemble the intended customer where feasible, explain that nothing will be submitted, and name a human reviewer who can check outputs and stop the exercise. The immediate question is whether people can complete and understand the proposed flow, not whether the business is ready to launch it.

Set the time and spending limits before inviting participants or buying tools. Record a comparable baseline for the current enquiry process, including customer effort and the owner's checking and correction work. MLAI's workflow-selection guide recommends observing the existing process and separating setup from recurring effort. If you have no comparable baseline, write “not measured” and collect it before claiming an improvement.

subsections.heading: Fill in the pilot scorecard
paragraphs: Copy this scorecard and fill in the plan before running the rehearsal. The tasks and decision rules below are a planning exercise for the hypothetical garden-tidy example, not a validated assessment method. Set your own thresholds against the baseline and the limits your business can afford.
Current workflow and comparison: Current workflow [ ]; comparable task or scenario [ ]; observation period or rehearsal count [ ].
Baseline measures: Customer completion time [ ]; owner review and correction time [ ]; complete and accurate requests [ ] out of [ ]. Record “not measured” wherever evidence is missing.
Scope and dates: Shortlisted use case [ ]; start date [ ]; review date [ ]; participant count [ ]; task count [ ].
Time and spending caps: Total setup, testing and revision cap [ ] hours; cash spending cap A$[ ].

Responsibility and data boundary: Named human reviewer with authority to stop [ ]; permitted tools [ ]; permitted synthetic inputs [ ]. Do not enter personal or confidential information into unapproved tools.

Proposed feedback tasks: Enter the supplied fictional garden-tidy request without coaching; change a detail on review; recover from a missing-field error; explain what the final screen means. Record any behaviour that must be simulated manually.
Feedback record: Task completed [ ]; assistance needed [ ]; misunderstandings [ ]; suggested changes [ ].
Time measures: Customer time per comparable task [ ]; owner review and correction time [ ]; combined handling time [ ]. Keep setup and revision time [ ] hours separate.
Quality measures: Correct and complete tasks [ ] out of [ ]; critical errors [ ]; unresolved issues [ ].
Actual spending: Tool expenses A$[ ]; participant expenses A$[ ]; other rehearsal expenses A$[ ]; total A$[ ].

Continue threshold: For this hypothetical rehearsal, proceed only to a bounded design or feasibility test if time meets [target against baseline], quality meets [required successful tasks out of total], unresolved critical errors equal zero, and both caps are respected.
Revise threshold: Retest a fixable time or quality miss only if the proposed correction [ ] and retest fit within the remaining time and spending caps.
Stop or pause threshold: Stop or pause if a privacy or safety concern arises, a cap would be exceeded, or the agreed revision still fails the thresholds.

During the rehearsal, record what participants do and where they need help, rather than relying on whether they like the screens. If the owner manually rehearses receiving and assessing a request, label that handling as simulated. Do not count a simulated integration as working. Keep the customer's effort, the owner's effort and preparation time visible so that a quicker screen journey does not hide extra review work.

No results or benchmark thresholds are supplied here. Rehearsal timings do not establish production savings, future operating costs or customer demand, and positive usability feedback does not authorise deployment.

sections.heading: Shortlist one use case and prepare your peer questions
paragraphs: Write down your shortlisted use case as a hypothesis. For the hypothetical garden-maintenance business: “Explore whether a three-screen quote-request flow helps prospective garden-tidy customers supply reviewable job details, with a person assessing every request.” This remains an idea to test, not evidence of customer demand.

Gather your prototype or preview, issue log and unrun pilot scorecard so a peer can see what you propose to test. Include an unresolved limitation, such as simulated rather than functioning field validation, and name the decision the rehearsal should inform: whether to continue to a bounded feasibility test, revise the design or stop. Peer experience can help identify gaps, but it does not replace intended-customer feedback, measured results or appropriate implementation review.

blocks.purpose: Place the data and accountability boundary immediately before the reader copies a prompt into a tool, where it can change their behaviour.
blocks.brief: In two short sentences, instruct readers to use synthetic inputs and never enter confidential or personal information into an unapproved tool; require human review of generated outputs. Make clear that this is a precaution for the exercise, not a statement that synthetic data or tool approval proves privacy compliance. Keep the full warning here rather than repeating it in adjacent prose.
blocks.title: Keep real customer data out

props.text: Use synthetic inputs, and never enter personal or confidential information into an unapproved tool. Have a person review all generated copy and interactions before relying on them.

faq.rationale: The body answers the relevant beginner questions about tool capabilities, manual linking, synthetic data, prototype limitations, review and pilot decisions. No distinct unanswered questions justify a repetitive FAQ.

layout.rationale: Use a restrained layout built around the article's actual working materials: an inline reusable prompt, a concise pilot-scorecard table and three peer questions. One warning earns a decorative block because it appears at the point of data entry. Omit a step list because the prose already carries the four-phase sequence; omit audience cards because there is one reader; omit quotes because no supported counter-intuitive finding needs a separate spotlight. Honour feedback against generic resource and template CTAs by keeping the working aids on-page. The optional events link follows the completed task in ordinary conclusion prose. Do not plan the system-rendered hero, table of contents, references, disclaimer, company CTA, author bio or footer. No example-page statistics were supplied, so density follows the task and available evidence rather than an invented page-length target.

claim_bindings.claim_text: For this hypothetical garden-tidy prototype, start with the normal route using the supplied synthetic details: enter the request, review it and open the simulated acknowledgement.

A drawn error message does not demonstrate functioning validation.

Mark checks the tool cannot support as “not testable here”.
These are practical checks for this exercise, not a comprehensive accessibility audit, security assessment or proof of operational reliability.

Plan a usability rehearsal with synthetic information, not a live quote-request service.

{/*cf-review:field-732e4a1cb08548209030fff66fc2b5a3*/"Start with one customer task, not a whole product"}

{TOPIC} — {/*cf-review:field-e220b894cc114559a0dd75bedb470976*/"For a hypothetical first prototype, give an artificial intelligence design assistant one customer task and ask for three connected screens using fictional data. Inspect the generated copy and interactions yourself, then define a small, capped pilot before buying tools or commissioning development. Start with the business problem rather than the software, consistent with business.gov.au\u2019s guidance on introducing AI."}

{/*cf-review:field-6f548a46cb384cbb84eb1b5446f42523*/"Here, a design assistant means an AI tool you instruct to draft interface layouts, wording or screen specifications. Our hypothetical example is an Australian garden-maintenance business considering a quote-request option for one-off garden tidy-ups. No customer research, prototype testing or validation has been conducted for this example."}

{/*cf-review:field-ede08fb0808649828a1a7419e92e07ab*/"AI can help design that flow without being part of the eventual service. A person could still assess every quote request, and the finished form might not need AI at all. A clickable prototype does not establish readiness for live use, secure data handling, functioning integrations or customer demand."}

{/*cf-review:field-e6bfdcb676f14a4eaee3b364e0ed301d*/"Choose one problem and draw its boundaries"}

{/*cf-review:field-853ac952ec0042bc89b2e61f9e1ecf57*/"Business.gov.au recommends identifying the business problem first and looking at software you already use when considering solutions. Use this sentence to narrow your idea: \u201c[Customer] needs to [complete task] so that [specific outcome]; we will explore whether [proposed change] helps.\u201d The outcome should be something a person can review, rather than a promise that the tool will deliver a business result."}

{/*cf-review:field-884c1ba62fd84da29cf278c046668fe5*/"For the hypothetical garden-maintenance business: \u201cA prospective garden-tidy customer needs to provide enough job information for a person to assess a quote request; we will explore whether a guided request form helps.\u201d Assume the current alternative is a phone or email enquiry. Keep the proposed offering to a request for a one-off garden tidy-up, with a person deciding what happens next."}

{/*cf-review:field-2833da643d6e48198d126594a7b34928*/"In this hypothetical exercise, limit the demonstration to three primary screens: enter job details, review and edit those details, then view a clearly labelled simulated acknowledgement. Leave out payments, accounts, live availability, automatic prices and connections to customer-management systems. The final screen should say \u201cDemo only\u2014nothing has been sent\u201d to make its simulated status explicit. During the rehearsal, ask participants what that message means and record any misunderstanding about whether a request or booking was made."}

{/*cf-review:field-1b2f85c5749542449500b216a4255ae0*/"Before generating anything, check whether an existing business-approved tool supports editable screens, linked buttons and a preview. Confirm its current access, sharing, export and pricing restrictions rather than assuming these features are included. Record tool limitations before deciding whether another subscription is needed."}

{"Use synthetic inputs, and never enter personal or confidential information into an unapproved tool. Have a person review all generated copy and interactions before relying on them."}

{/*cf-review:field-c60f6cd8635b4219a03b0f95cf1663ac*/"Generate the screens and connect the flow"}

{/*cf-review:field-67e81da8dab1458db89ef792833479d8*/"Give the assistant the customer task, the information it can use, the output you want and the limits it must respect. OpenAI Academy\u2019s small-business workshop calls these Goal, Context, Output and Boundary. They help you explain the request without needing technical language. The hypothetical garden-tidy exercise below applies that structure; it does not assume your chosen tool can generate working, clickable screens."}

{/*cf-review:field-e8a8c252a1d247dd8b5d4c3ad56cb416*/"Check what the assistant actually returns. A screen specification describes the layout, words and behaviour. A static image shows an appearance but has no working controls. A clickable prototype connects screens so someone can follow a route. If the assistant supplies only copy, layouts, specifications or images, use them to assemble editable screens in an already-approved design or presentation tool."}

{/*cf-review:field-9dc957bc72aa48808309274b1e485a4d*/"Copy and adapt this prompt"}

{/*cf-review:field-6539bc71e95e4f4aa5c0a60dfa7505fb*/"Replace the bracketed descriptions with your intended business, customer and task. The supplied sample details belong to the hypothetical garden-tidy example and are synthetic, not customer records."}

{/*cf-review:field-53b702321abe4bd1af51832ca9e0bf3b*/"Act as a design assistant for [small business and proposed offering]. Intended user: [customer]. Task: [one customer task]. For this hypothetical exercise, create a low-fidelity, mobile-first prototype with exactly three primary screens: (1) enter the necessary details, (2) review them and edit, and (3) view a simulated acknowledgement. Keep the layout simple and suitable for a narrow phone screen."}

{/*cf-review:field-8a7785c7c26c4b6c9915a3d9af930fa0*/"For this hypothetical garden-tidy example, use only these synthetic details: Sample Customer A; demo@example.com; service: one-off garden tidy; garden size: small; job note: weed beds and sweep paths. Include labelled fields, concise plain-English copy, a missing-required-field state and an invalid-email state within the relevant screen. Specify forward, edit/back and restart interactions. Use readable text and errors that do not rely on colour alone."}

{/*cf-review:field-8372339b701141e290bc273c92dc2715*/"Do not create real accounts, send messages, store submissions, connect services, quote prices or promise availability. Label the final screen: Demo only\u2014nothing has been sent. Output editable screens and an interaction map if supported; otherwise provide a screen specification and exact linking instructions. List assumptions, simulated behaviours and anything requiring human review. Do not invent customer findings."}

{/*cf-review:field-69c940251cf64bacb1cd4b416d11f7fe*/"Connect the screens and check the preview"}

{/*cf-review:field-f856acf6cc704cea84196c3564710be2*/"For the hypothetical garden-tidy flow, link the job-details screen to the review screen. From review, provide an edit action that returns to job details and a simulated submission action that opens the acknowledgement. Let the acknowledgement restart the demonstration. If the tool has not created those links, connect the buttons manually where supported, then follow each route in preview or presentation mode."}

{/*cf-review:field-74c4d5f21093458384443e3d0bfb3de2*/"Links alone do not prove that form behaviour works. If the prototype cannot accept typed details, label that behaviour as simulated and record the limitation."}

{/*cf-review:field-bbb3c16921e54adea53003f7a5063ec3*/"Walk through the prototype before showing it to anyone"}

{/*cf-review:field-b8187ffde3534eafa885171d6d3d0957*/"Inspect the generated screens yourself rather than accepting the assistant\u2019s claim that they work. Business.gov.au advises checking AI-generated information before relying on it. For this hypothetical garden-tidy prototype, start with the normal route using the supplied synthetic details: enter the request, review it and open the simulated acknowledgement. Check that necessary details are requested before review, the review matches the input and every button reaches its intended destination."}

{/*cf-review:field-1952efe8ae464f70b94be2bbf9f59dbb*/"Then try the correction routes. Leave a required field blank, enter an invalid fictional email address, return from review to change the garden size, then restart the demonstration. Keep a short issue log recording the route, expected behaviour, observed behaviour and anything you simulated manually. A drawn error message does not demonstrate functioning validation. If the prototype cannot preserve edited values or respond to invalid input, record that limitation rather than treating the route as passed."}

{/*cf-review:field-4be734afddd847c892146afc9bcd6d54*/"Read the copy alongside those interactions. Look for unexplained fields, missing instructions and promises about prices, availability or messages being sent that the demonstration cannot fulfil. Where \u201cContinue\u201d leaves the destination unclear, use a label such as \u201cReview job details\u201d. Check that the acknowledgement describes a simulation, not a real quote request or booking, and that returning to edit is easy to find."}

{/*cf-review:field-2d63f3610f5a4c55a6f5a343369ef7bc*/"Open a narrow mobile preview and inspect it for clipped content, readable text and enough spacing to distinguish adjacent buttons. Where the tool permits, try keyboard navigation and zoom, and check whether keyboard focus remains visible. Inspect field labels and make sure errors explain the problem in words rather than relying on colour alone. Mark checks the tool cannot support as \u201cnot testable here\u201d. These are practical checks for this exercise, not a comprehensive accessibility audit, security assessment or proof of operational reliability."}

{/*cf-review:field-7ff25ec5353b47bda0ecf5562d8a1b7c*/"Ask for a bounded revision, then repeat the affected route. For example, in this hypothetical prototype: \u201cOn the review screen, add an Edit job details action that returns to the entry screen; keep all other copy unchanged.\u201d Check the revised copy and links yourself, and update the issue log with what changed, what remains unresolved and what is still simulated."}

{/*cf-review:field-f5fabdfa8e1447659331d3b193f31ff8*/"Draft a capped pilot before committing money"}

{/*cf-review:field-c46d85d2a8844c9c9762073acf87cd64*/"Plan a usability rehearsal with synthetic information, not a live quote-request service. For the hypothetical garden-tidy offering, invite willing participants who resemble the intended customer where feasible, explain that nothing will be submitted, and name a human reviewer who can check outputs and stop the exercise. The immediate question is whether people can complete and understand the proposed flow, not whether the business is ready to launch it."}

{/*cf-review:field-8e1e20ac0f924c5a907364e03db448a7*/"Set the time and spending limits before inviting participants or buying tools. Record a comparable baseline for the current enquiry process, including customer effort and the owner's checking and correction work. MLAI's workflow-selection guide recommends observing the existing process and separating setup from recurring effort. If you have no comparable baseline, write \u201cnot measured\u201d and collect it before claiming an improvement."}

{/*cf-review:field-413fc18402654e56b13082815fde80c9*/"Fill in the pilot scorecard"}

{/*cf-review:field-892349cbbedd42869aa24587505fc7b4*/"Copy this scorecard and fill in the plan before running the rehearsal. The tasks and decision rules below are a planning exercise for the hypothetical garden-tidy example, not a validated assessment method. Set your own thresholds against the baseline and the limits your business can afford."}

{/*cf-review:field-d996ef4b80fc4d04b1a7c6fa16e738a5*/"Current workflow and comparison: Current workflow [ ]; comparable task or scenario [ ]; observation period or rehearsal count [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-e824e1a769284adb92f8ec54f06541f0*/"Baseline measures: Customer completion time [ ]; owner review and correction time [ ]; complete and accurate requests [ ] out of [ ]. Record \u201cnot measured\u201d wherever evidence is missing."}

{/*cf-review:field-b5a5a07276bc44969e31a9a9cddabb81*/"Scope and dates: Shortlisted use case [ ]; start date [ ]; review date [ ]; participant count [ ]; task count [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-ae57d39ce0ad43ad8ee53319260b0c5d*/"Time and spending caps: Total setup, testing and revision cap [ ] hours; cash spending cap A$[ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-8868f83fe35d428898586ece4a391e5b*/"Responsibility and data boundary: Named human reviewer with authority to stop [ ]; permitted tools [ ]; permitted synthetic inputs [ ]. Do not enter personal or confidential information into unapproved tools."}

{/*cf-review:field-512bb98225c14bf3b5a66cea3d86ae37*/"Proposed feedback tasks: Enter the supplied fictional garden-tidy request without coaching; change a detail on review; recover from a missing-field error; explain what the final screen means. Record any behaviour that must be simulated manually."}

{/*cf-review:field-4b3b85e9176c4a5b8c778daa66fbb690*/"Feedback record: Task completed [ ]; assistance needed [ ]; misunderstandings [ ]; suggested changes [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-7b04ee29997a4165ade274a93ebbbfb2*/"Time measures: Customer time per comparable task [ ]; owner review and correction time [ ]; combined handling time [ ]. Keep setup and revision time [ ] hours separate."}

{/*cf-review:field-db5bc86ba2bf4d84b876de099bc12cf6*/"Quality measures: Correct and complete tasks [ ] out of [ ]; critical errors [ ]; unresolved issues [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-6e771221d38149b2b86404d7990cafda*/"Actual spending: Tool expenses A$[ ]; participant expenses A$[ ]; other rehearsal expenses A$[ ]; total A$[ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-d2ad80a7b7864d2d8b8d391fc905035d*/"Continue threshold: For this hypothetical rehearsal, proceed only to a bounded design or feasibility test if time meets [target against baseline], quality meets [required successful tasks out of total], unresolved critical errors equal zero, and both caps are respected."}

{/*cf-review:field-01a77f85f5ea43e1a4d3f7c16af01cba*/"Revise threshold: Retest a fixable time or quality miss only if the proposed correction [ ] and retest fit within the remaining time and spending caps."}

{/*cf-review:field-08c024210dd04db3afc884ec59990bce*/"Stop or pause threshold: Stop or pause if a privacy or safety concern arises, a cap would be exceeded, or the agreed revision still fails the thresholds."}

{/*cf-review:field-75ab7e6c479043dab04ea0ef78ad192c*/"During the rehearsal, record what participants do and where they need help, rather than relying on whether they like the screens. If the owner manually rehearses receiving and assessing a request, label that handling as simulated. Do not count a simulated integration as working. Keep the customer's effort, the owner's effort and preparation time visible so that a quicker screen journey does not hide extra review work."}

{/*cf-review:field-e7f4cc599a7e4a30bf7f513ad149864c*/"No results or benchmark thresholds are supplied here. Rehearsal timings do not establish production savings, future operating costs or customer demand, and positive usability feedback does not authorise deployment."}

{/*cf-review:field-1e41ae7f42c04e7ea9d8d5f11b4443f6*/"Shortlist one use case and prepare your peer questions"}

{/*cf-review:field-c9c03f796c564503b4deb32f114bee7f*/"Write down your shortlisted use case as a hypothesis. For the hypothetical garden-maintenance business: \u201cExplore whether a three-screen quote-request flow helps prospective garden-tidy customers supply reviewable job details, with a person assessing every request.\u201d This remains an idea to test, not evidence of customer demand."}

{/*cf-review:field-98a4ae1532254986b40302db0a551e8b*/"Gather your prototype or preview, issue log and unrun pilot scorecard so a peer can see what you propose to test. Include an unresolved limitation, such as simulated rather than functioning field validation, and name the decision the rehearsal should inform: whether to continue to a bounded feasibility test, revise the design or stop. Peer experience can help identify gaps, but it does not replace intended-customer feedback, measured results or appropriate implementation review."}

  • {/*cf-review:field-eea273ab1be54d83848ce191bf1b122d*/"Which editing, validation, mobile, sharing or export limitations should I check in my current tools?"}

{/*cf-review:field-b874d2ad558e4bfcac2da7bd951affcc*/"Optional next step for a peer conversation"}

{/*cf-review:field-ee390030ceab4bf4a4309885d5636f40*/"Explore MLAI events if you\u2019d like a peer conversation about your shortlisted use case and questions. Event availability, format and cost vary, so check the current listing and the organiser\u2019s details before deciding whether to attend."}

{/*cf-review:field-2d2d2b9df1f447fa8610d305e8e0350c*/"Attendance does not guarantee individual implementation advice. You can continue your bounded planning and feedback work without attending."}

{/*cf-review:field-732e4a1cb08548209030fff66fc2b5a3*/"Start with one customer task, not a whole product"}

{TOPIC} — {/*cf-review:field-e220b894cc114559a0dd75bedb470976*/"For a hypothetical first prototype, give an artificial intelligence design assistant one customer task and ask for three connected screens using fictional data. Inspect the generated copy and interactions yourself, then define a small, capped pilot before buying tools or commissioning development. Start with the business problem rather than the software, consistent with business.gov.au\u2019s guidance on introducing AI."}

{/*cf-review:field-6f548a46cb384cbb84eb1b5446f42523*/"Here, a design assistant means an AI tool you instruct to draft interface layouts, wording or screen specifications. Our hypothetical example is an Australian garden-maintenance business considering a quote-request option for one-off garden tidy-ups. No customer research, prototype testing or validation has been conducted for this example."}

{/*cf-review:field-ede08fb0808649828a1a7419e92e07ab*/"AI can help design that flow without being part of the eventual service. A person could still assess every quote request, and the finished form might not need AI at all. A clickable prototype does not establish readiness for live use, secure data handling, functioning integrations or customer demand."}

{/*cf-review:field-e6bfdcb676f14a4eaee3b364e0ed301d*/"Choose one problem and draw its boundaries"}

{/*cf-review:field-853ac952ec0042bc89b2e61f9e1ecf57*/"Business.gov.au recommends identifying the business problem first and looking at software you already use when considering solutions. Use this sentence to narrow your idea: \u201c[Customer] needs to [complete task] so that [specific outcome]; we will explore whether [proposed change] helps.\u201d The outcome should be something a person can review, rather than a promise that the tool will deliver a business result."}

{/*cf-review:field-884c1ba62fd84da29cf278c046668fe5*/"For the hypothetical garden-maintenance business: \u201cA prospective garden-tidy customer needs to provide enough job information for a person to assess a quote request; we will explore whether a guided request form helps.\u201d Assume the current alternative is a phone or email enquiry. Keep the proposed offering to a request for a one-off garden tidy-up, with a person deciding what happens next."}

{/*cf-review:field-2833da643d6e48198d126594a7b34928*/"In this hypothetical exercise, limit the demonstration to three primary screens: enter job details, review and edit those details, then view a clearly labelled simulated acknowledgement. Leave out payments, accounts, live availability, automatic prices and connections to customer-management systems. The final screen should say \u201cDemo only\u2014nothing has been sent\u201d to make its simulated status explicit. During the rehearsal, ask participants what that message means and record any misunderstanding about whether a request or booking was made."}

{/*cf-review:field-1b2f85c5749542449500b216a4255ae0*/"Before generating anything, check whether an existing business-approved tool supports editable screens, linked buttons and a preview. Confirm its current access, sharing, export and pricing restrictions rather than assuming these features are included. Record tool limitations before deciding whether another subscription is needed."}

{"Use synthetic inputs, and never enter personal or confidential information into an unapproved tool. Have a person review all generated copy and interactions before relying on them."}

{/*cf-review:field-c60f6cd8635b4219a03b0f95cf1663ac*/"Generate the screens and connect the flow"}

{/*cf-review:field-67e81da8dab1458db89ef792833479d8*/"Give the assistant the customer task, the information it can use, the output you want and the limits it must respect. OpenAI Academy\u2019s small-business workshop calls these Goal, Context, Output and Boundary. They help you explain the request without needing technical language. The hypothetical garden-tidy exercise below applies that structure; it does not assume your chosen tool can generate working, clickable screens."}

{/*cf-review:field-e8a8c252a1d247dd8b5d4c3ad56cb416*/"Check what the assistant actually returns. A screen specification describes the layout, words and behaviour. A static image shows an appearance but has no working controls. A clickable prototype connects screens so someone can follow a route. If the assistant supplies only copy, layouts, specifications or images, use them to assemble editable screens in an already-approved design or presentation tool."}

{/*cf-review:field-9dc957bc72aa48808309274b1e485a4d*/"Copy and adapt this prompt"}

{/*cf-review:field-6539bc71e95e4f4aa5c0a60dfa7505fb*/"Replace the bracketed descriptions with your intended business, customer and task. The supplied sample details belong to the hypothetical garden-tidy example and are synthetic, not customer records."}

{/*cf-review:field-53b702321abe4bd1af51832ca9e0bf3b*/"Act as a design assistant for [small business and proposed offering]. Intended user: [customer]. Task: [one customer task]. For this hypothetical exercise, create a low-fidelity, mobile-first prototype with exactly three primary screens: (1) enter the necessary details, (2) review them and edit, and (3) view a simulated acknowledgement. Keep the layout simple and suitable for a narrow phone screen."}

{/*cf-review:field-8a7785c7c26c4b6c9915a3d9af930fa0*/"For this hypothetical garden-tidy example, use only these synthetic details: Sample Customer A; demo@example.com; service: one-off garden tidy; garden size: small; job note: weed beds and sweep paths. Include labelled fields, concise plain-English copy, a missing-required-field state and an invalid-email state within the relevant screen. Specify forward, edit/back and restart interactions. Use readable text and errors that do not rely on colour alone."}

{/*cf-review:field-8372339b701141e290bc273c92dc2715*/"Do not create real accounts, send messages, store submissions, connect services, quote prices or promise availability. Label the final screen: Demo only\u2014nothing has been sent. Output editable screens and an interaction map if supported; otherwise provide a screen specification and exact linking instructions. List assumptions, simulated behaviours and anything requiring human review. Do not invent customer findings."}

{/*cf-review:field-69c940251cf64bacb1cd4b416d11f7fe*/"Connect the screens and check the preview"}

{/*cf-review:field-f856acf6cc704cea84196c3564710be2*/"For the hypothetical garden-tidy flow, link the job-details screen to the review screen. From review, provide an edit action that returns to job details and a simulated submission action that opens the acknowledgement. Let the acknowledgement restart the demonstration. If the tool has not created those links, connect the buttons manually where supported, then follow each route in preview or presentation mode."}

{/*cf-review:field-74c4d5f21093458384443e3d0bfb3de2*/"Links alone do not prove that form behaviour works. If the prototype cannot accept typed details, label that behaviour as simulated and record the limitation."}

{/*cf-review:field-bbb3c16921e54adea53003f7a5063ec3*/"Walk through the prototype before showing it to anyone"}

{/*cf-review:field-b8187ffde3534eafa885171d6d3d0957*/"Inspect the generated screens yourself rather than accepting the assistant\u2019s claim that they work. Business.gov.au advises checking AI-generated information before relying on it. For this hypothetical garden-tidy prototype, start with the normal route using the supplied synthetic details: enter the request, review it and open the simulated acknowledgement. Check that necessary details are requested before review, the review matches the input and every button reaches its intended destination."}

{/*cf-review:field-1952efe8ae464f70b94be2bbf9f59dbb*/"Then try the correction routes. Leave a required field blank, enter an invalid fictional email address, return from review to change the garden size, then restart the demonstration. Keep a short issue log recording the route, expected behaviour, observed behaviour and anything you simulated manually. A drawn error message does not demonstrate functioning validation. If the prototype cannot preserve edited values or respond to invalid input, record that limitation rather than treating the route as passed."}

{/*cf-review:field-4be734afddd847c892146afc9bcd6d54*/"Read the copy alongside those interactions. Look for unexplained fields, missing instructions and promises about prices, availability or messages being sent that the demonstration cannot fulfil. Where \u201cContinue\u201d leaves the destination unclear, use a label such as \u201cReview job details\u201d. Check that the acknowledgement describes a simulation, not a real quote request or booking, and that returning to edit is easy to find."}

{/*cf-review:field-2d63f3610f5a4c55a6f5a343369ef7bc*/"Open a narrow mobile preview and inspect it for clipped content, readable text and enough spacing to distinguish adjacent buttons. Where the tool permits, try keyboard navigation and zoom, and check whether keyboard focus remains visible. Inspect field labels and make sure errors explain the problem in words rather than relying on colour alone. Mark checks the tool cannot support as \u201cnot testable here\u201d. These are practical checks for this exercise, not a comprehensive accessibility audit, security assessment or proof of operational reliability."}

{/*cf-review:field-7ff25ec5353b47bda0ecf5562d8a1b7c*/"Ask for a bounded revision, then repeat the affected route. For example, in this hypothetical prototype: \u201cOn the review screen, add an Edit job details action that returns to the entry screen; keep all other copy unchanged.\u201d Check the revised copy and links yourself, and update the issue log with what changed, what remains unresolved and what is still simulated."}

{/*cf-review:field-f5fabdfa8e1447659331d3b193f31ff8*/"Draft a capped pilot before committing money"}

{/*cf-review:field-c46d85d2a8844c9c9762073acf87cd64*/"Plan a usability rehearsal with synthetic information, not a live quote-request service. For the hypothetical garden-tidy offering, invite willing participants who resemble the intended customer where feasible, explain that nothing will be submitted, and name a human reviewer who can check outputs and stop the exercise. The immediate question is whether people can complete and understand the proposed flow, not whether the business is ready to launch it."}

{/*cf-review:field-8e1e20ac0f924c5a907364e03db448a7*/"Set the time and spending limits before inviting participants or buying tools. Record a comparable baseline for the current enquiry process, including customer effort and the owner's checking and correction work. MLAI's workflow-selection guide recommends observing the existing process and separating setup from recurring effort. If you have no comparable baseline, write \u201cnot measured\u201d and collect it before claiming an improvement."}

{/*cf-review:field-413fc18402654e56b13082815fde80c9*/"Fill in the pilot scorecard"}

{/*cf-review:field-892349cbbedd42869aa24587505fc7b4*/"Copy this scorecard and fill in the plan before running the rehearsal. The tasks and decision rules below are a planning exercise for the hypothetical garden-tidy example, not a validated assessment method. Set your own thresholds against the baseline and the limits your business can afford."}

{/*cf-review:field-d996ef4b80fc4d04b1a7c6fa16e738a5*/"Current workflow and comparison: Current workflow [ ]; comparable task or scenario [ ]; observation period or rehearsal count [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-e824e1a769284adb92f8ec54f06541f0*/"Baseline measures: Customer completion time [ ]; owner review and correction time [ ]; complete and accurate requests [ ] out of [ ]. Record \u201cnot measured\u201d wherever evidence is missing."}

{/*cf-review:field-b5a5a07276bc44969e31a9a9cddabb81*/"Scope and dates: Shortlisted use case [ ]; start date [ ]; review date [ ]; participant count [ ]; task count [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-ae57d39ce0ad43ad8ee53319260b0c5d*/"Time and spending caps: Total setup, testing and revision cap [ ] hours; cash spending cap A$[ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-8868f83fe35d428898586ece4a391e5b*/"Responsibility and data boundary: Named human reviewer with authority to stop [ ]; permitted tools [ ]; permitted synthetic inputs [ ]. Do not enter personal or confidential information into unapproved tools."}

{/*cf-review:field-512bb98225c14bf3b5a66cea3d86ae37*/"Proposed feedback tasks: Enter the supplied fictional garden-tidy request without coaching; change a detail on review; recover from a missing-field error; explain what the final screen means. Record any behaviour that must be simulated manually."}

{/*cf-review:field-4b3b85e9176c4a5b8c778daa66fbb690*/"Feedback record: Task completed [ ]; assistance needed [ ]; misunderstandings [ ]; suggested changes [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-7b04ee29997a4165ade274a93ebbbfb2*/"Time measures: Customer time per comparable task [ ]; owner review and correction time [ ]; combined handling time [ ]. Keep setup and revision time [ ] hours separate."}

{/*cf-review:field-db5bc86ba2bf4d84b876de099bc12cf6*/"Quality measures: Correct and complete tasks [ ] out of [ ]; critical errors [ ]; unresolved issues [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-6e771221d38149b2b86404d7990cafda*/"Actual spending: Tool expenses A$[ ]; participant expenses A$[ ]; other rehearsal expenses A$[ ]; total A$[ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-d2ad80a7b7864d2d8b8d391fc905035d*/"Continue threshold: For this hypothetical rehearsal, proceed only to a bounded design or feasibility test if time meets [target against baseline], quality meets [required successful tasks out of total], unresolved critical errors equal zero, and both caps are respected."}

{/*cf-review:field-01a77f85f5ea43e1a4d3f7c16af01cba*/"Revise threshold: Retest a fixable time or quality miss only if the proposed correction [ ] and retest fit within the remaining time and spending caps."}

{/*cf-review:field-08c024210dd04db3afc884ec59990bce*/"Stop or pause threshold: Stop or pause if a privacy or safety concern arises, a cap would be exceeded, or the agreed revision still fails the thresholds."}

{/*cf-review:field-75ab7e6c479043dab04ea0ef78ad192c*/"During the rehearsal, record what participants do and where they need help, rather than relying on whether they like the screens. If the owner manually rehearses receiving and assessing a request, label that handling as simulated. Do not count a simulated integration as working. Keep the customer's effort, the owner's effort and preparation time visible so that a quicker screen journey does not hide extra review work."}

{/*cf-review:field-e7f4cc599a7e4a30bf7f513ad149864c*/"No results or benchmark thresholds are supplied here. Rehearsal timings do not establish production savings, future operating costs or customer demand, and positive usability feedback does not authorise deployment."}

{/*cf-review:field-1e41ae7f42c04e7ea9d8d5f11b4443f6*/"Shortlist one use case and prepare your peer questions"}

{/*cf-review:field-c9c03f796c564503b4deb32f114bee7f*/"Write down your shortlisted use case as a hypothesis. For the hypothetical garden-maintenance business: \u201cExplore whether a three-screen quote-request flow helps prospective garden-tidy customers supply reviewable job details, with a person assessing every request.\u201d This remains an idea to test, not evidence of customer demand."}

{/*cf-review:field-98a4ae1532254986b40302db0a551e8b*/"Gather your prototype or preview, issue log and unrun pilot scorecard so a peer can see what you propose to test. Include an unresolved limitation, such as simulated rather than functioning field validation, and name the decision the rehearsal should inform: whether to continue to a bounded feasibility test, revise the design or stop. Peer experience can help identify gaps, but it does not replace intended-customer feedback, measured results or appropriate implementation review."}

  • {/*cf-review:field-9481dca510ea433b9b6e3487dc70ef0b*/"What would have to work beyond these screens before this flow could be used for real requests?"}
  • {/*cf-review:field-eea273ab1be54d83848ce191bf1b122d*/"Which editing, validation, mobile, sharing or export limitations should I check in my current tools?"}
  • {/*cf-review:field-480f58d6440541a0b791e3d0547ee0a5*/"Are my baseline, task count, review-time accounting and continue, revise or stop thresholds useful for this small rehearsal?"}

{/*cf-review:field-b874d2ad558e4bfcac2da7bd951affcc*/"Optional next step for a peer conversation"}

{/*cf-review:field-ee390030ceab4bf4a4309885d5636f40*/"Explore MLAI events if you\u2019d like a peer conversation about your shortlisted use case and questions. Event availability, format and cost vary, so check the current listing and the organiser\u2019s details before deciding whether to attend."}

{/*cf-review:field-2d2d2b9df1f447fa8610d305e8e0350c*/"Attendance does not guarantee individual implementation advice. You can continue your bounded planning and feedback work without attending."}
