{/*cf-review:field-732e4a1cb08548209030fff66fc2b5a3*/"Start with one customer task, not a whole product"}

{TOPIC} — {/*cf-review:field-e220b894cc114559a0dd75bedb470976*/"For a hypothetical first prototype, give an artificial intelligence design assistant one customer task and ask for three connected screens using fictional data. Inspect the generated copy and interactions yourself, then define a small, capped pilot before buying tools or commissioning development. Start with the business problem rather than the software, consistent with business.gov.au\u2019s guidance on introducing AI."}

{/*cf-review:field-6f548a46cb384cbb84eb1b5446f42523*/"Here, a design assistant means an AI tool you instruct to draft interface layouts, wording or screen specifications. Our hypothetical example is an Australian garden-maintenance business considering a quote-request option for one-off garden tidy-ups. No customer research, prototype testing or validation has been conducted for this example."}

{/*cf-review:field-ede08fb0808649828a1a7419e92e07ab*/"AI can help design that flow without being part of the eventual service. A person could still assess every quote request, and the finished form might not need AI at all. A clickable prototype does not establish readiness for live use, secure data handling, functioning integrations or customer demand."}

{/*cf-review:field-e6bfdcb676f14a4eaee3b364e0ed301d*/"Choose one problem and draw its boundaries"}

{/*cf-review:field-853ac952ec0042bc89b2e61f9e1ecf57*/"Business.gov.au recommends identifying the business problem first and looking at software you already use when considering solutions. Use this sentence to narrow your idea: \u201c[Customer] needs to [complete task] so that [specific outcome]; we will explore whether [proposed change] helps.\u201d The outcome should be something a person can review, rather than a promise that the tool will deliver a business result."}

{/*cf-review:field-884c1ba62fd84da29cf278c046668fe5*/"For the hypothetical garden-maintenance business: \u201cA prospective garden-tidy customer needs to provide enough job information for a person to assess a quote request; we will explore whether a guided request form helps.\u201d Assume the current alternative is a phone or email enquiry. Keep the proposed offering to a request for a one-off garden tidy-up, with a person deciding what happens next."}

{/*cf-review:field-2833da643d6e48198d126594a7b34928*/"In this hypothetical exercise, limit the demonstration to three primary screens: enter job details, review and edit those details, then view a clearly labelled simulated acknowledgement. Leave out payments, accounts, live availability, automatic prices and connections to customer-management systems. The final screen should say \u201cDemo only\u2014nothing has been sent\u201d to make its simulated status explicit. During the rehearsal, ask participants what that message means and record any misunderstanding about whether a request or booking was made."}

{/*cf-review:field-1b2f85c5749542449500b216a4255ae0*/"Before generating anything, check whether an existing business-approved tool supports editable screens, linked buttons and a preview. Confirm its current access, sharing, export and pricing restrictions rather than assuming these features are included. Record tool limitations before deciding whether another subscription is needed."}

{"Use synthetic inputs, and never enter personal or confidential information into an unapproved tool. Have a person review all generated copy and interactions before relying on them."}

{/*cf-review:field-c60f6cd8635b4219a03b0f95cf1663ac*/"Generate the screens and connect the flow"}

{/*cf-review:field-67e81da8dab1458db89ef792833479d8*/"Give the assistant the customer task, the information it can use, the output you want and the limits it must respect. OpenAI Academy\u2019s small-business workshop calls these Goal, Context, Output and Boundary. They help you explain the request without needing technical language. The hypothetical garden-tidy exercise below applies that structure; it does not assume your chosen tool can generate working, clickable screens."}

{/*cf-review:field-e8a8c252a1d247dd8b5d4c3ad56cb416*/"Check what the assistant actually returns. A screen specification describes the layout, words and behaviour. A static image shows an appearance but has no working controls. A clickable prototype connects screens so someone can follow a route. If the assistant supplies only copy, layouts, specifications or images, use them to assemble editable screens in an already-approved design or presentation tool."}

{/*cf-review:field-9dc957bc72aa48808309274b1e485a4d*/"Copy and adapt this prompt"}

{/*cf-review:field-6539bc71e95e4f4aa5c0a60dfa7505fb*/"Replace the bracketed descriptions with your intended business, customer and task. The supplied sample details belong to the hypothetical garden-tidy example and are synthetic, not customer records."}

{/*cf-review:field-53b702321abe4bd1af51832ca9e0bf3b*/"Act as a design assistant for [small business and proposed offering]. Intended user: [customer]. Task: [one customer task]. For this hypothetical exercise, create a low-fidelity, mobile-first prototype with exactly three primary screens: (1) enter the necessary details, (2) review them and edit, and (3) view a simulated acknowledgement. Keep the layout simple and suitable for a narrow phone screen."}

{/*cf-review:field-8a7785c7c26c4b6c9915a3d9af930fa0*/"For this hypothetical garden-tidy example, use only these synthetic details: Sample Customer A; demo@example.com; service: one-off garden tidy; garden size: small; job note: weed beds and sweep paths. Include labelled fields, concise plain-English copy, a missing-required-field state and an invalid-email state within the relevant screen. Specify forward, edit/back and restart interactions. Use readable text and errors that do not rely on colour alone."}

{/*cf-review:field-8372339b701141e290bc273c92dc2715*/"Do not create real accounts, send messages, store submissions, connect services, quote prices or promise availability. Label the final screen: Demo only\u2014nothing has been sent. Output editable screens and an interaction map if supported; otherwise provide a screen specification and exact linking instructions. List assumptions, simulated behaviours and anything requiring human review. Do not invent customer findings."}

{/*cf-review:field-69c940251cf64bacb1cd4b416d11f7fe*/"Connect the screens and check the preview"}

{/*cf-review:field-f856acf6cc704cea84196c3564710be2*/"For the hypothetical garden-tidy flow, link the job-details screen to the review screen. From review, provide an edit action that returns to job details and a simulated submission action that opens the acknowledgement. Let the acknowledgement restart the demonstration. If the tool has not created those links, connect the buttons manually where supported, then follow each route in preview or presentation mode."}

{/*cf-review:field-74c4d5f21093458384443e3d0bfb3de2*/"Links alone do not prove that form behaviour works. If the prototype cannot accept typed details, label that behaviour as simulated and record the limitation."}

{/*cf-review:field-bbb3c16921e54adea53003f7a5063ec3*/"Walk through the prototype before showing it to anyone"}

{/*cf-review:field-b8187ffde3534eafa885171d6d3d0957*/"Inspect the generated screens yourself rather than accepting the assistant\u2019s claim that they work. Business.gov.au advises checking AI-generated information before relying on it. For this hypothetical garden-tidy prototype, start with the normal route using the supplied synthetic details: enter the request, review it and open the simulated acknowledgement. Check that necessary details are requested before review, the review matches the input and every button reaches its intended destination."}

{/*cf-review:field-1952efe8ae464f70b94be2bbf9f59dbb*/"Then try the correction routes. Leave a required field blank, enter an invalid fictional email address, return from review to change the garden size, then restart the demonstration. Keep a short issue log recording the route, expected behaviour, observed behaviour and anything you simulated manually. A drawn error message does not demonstrate functioning validation. If the prototype cannot preserve edited values or respond to invalid input, record that limitation rather than treating the route as passed."}

{/*cf-review:field-4be734afddd847c892146afc9bcd6d54*/"Read the copy alongside those interactions. Look for unexplained fields, missing instructions and promises about prices, availability or messages being sent that the demonstration cannot fulfil. Where \u201cContinue\u201d leaves the destination unclear, use a label such as \u201cReview job details\u201d. Check that the acknowledgement describes a simulation, not a real quote request or booking, and that returning to edit is easy to find."}

{/*cf-review:field-2d63f3610f5a4c55a6f5a343369ef7bc*/"Open a narrow mobile preview and inspect it for clipped content, readable text and enough spacing to distinguish adjacent buttons. Where the tool permits, try keyboard navigation and zoom, and check whether keyboard focus remains visible. Inspect field labels and make sure errors explain the problem in words rather than relying on colour alone. Mark checks the tool cannot support as \u201cnot testable here\u201d. These are practical checks for this exercise, not a comprehensive accessibility audit, security assessment or proof of operational reliability."}

{/*cf-review:field-7ff25ec5353b47bda0ecf5562d8a1b7c*/"Ask for a bounded revision, then repeat the affected route. For example, in this hypothetical prototype: \u201cOn the review screen, add an Edit job details action that returns to the entry screen; keep all other copy unchanged.\u201d Check the revised copy and links yourself, and update the issue log with what changed, what remains unresolved and what is still simulated."}

{/*cf-review:field-f5fabdfa8e1447659331d3b193f31ff8*/"Draft a capped pilot before committing money"}

{/*cf-review:field-c46d85d2a8844c9c9762073acf87cd64*/"Plan a usability rehearsal with synthetic information, not a live quote-request service. For the hypothetical garden-tidy offering, invite willing participants who resemble the intended customer where feasible, explain that nothing will be submitted, and name a human reviewer who can check outputs and stop the exercise. The immediate question is whether people can complete and understand the proposed flow, not whether the business is ready to launch it."}

{/*cf-review:field-8e1e20ac0f924c5a907364e03db448a7*/"Set the time and spending limits before inviting participants or buying tools. Record a comparable baseline for the current enquiry process, including customer effort and the owner's checking and correction work. MLAI's workflow-selection guide recommends observing the existing process and separating setup from recurring effort. If you have no comparable baseline, write \u201cnot measured\u201d and collect it before claiming an improvement."}

{/*cf-review:field-413fc18402654e56b13082815fde80c9*/"Fill in the pilot scorecard"}

{/*cf-review:field-892349cbbedd42869aa24587505fc7b4*/"Copy this scorecard and fill in the plan before running the rehearsal. The tasks and decision rules below are a planning exercise for the hypothetical garden-tidy example, not a validated assessment method. Set your own thresholds against the baseline and the limits your business can afford."}

{/*cf-review:field-d996ef4b80fc4d04b1a7c6fa16e738a5*/"Current workflow and comparison: Current workflow [ ]; comparable task or scenario [ ]; observation period or rehearsal count [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-e824e1a769284adb92f8ec54f06541f0*/"Baseline measures: Customer completion time [ ]; owner review and correction time [ ]; complete and accurate requests [ ] out of [ ]. Record \u201cnot measured\u201d wherever evidence is missing."}

{/*cf-review:field-b5a5a07276bc44969e31a9a9cddabb81*/"Scope and dates: Shortlisted use case [ ]; start date [ ]; review date [ ]; participant count [ ]; task count [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-ae57d39ce0ad43ad8ee53319260b0c5d*/"Time and spending caps: Total setup, testing and revision cap [ ] hours; cash spending cap A$[ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-8868f83fe35d428898586ece4a391e5b*/"Responsibility and data boundary: Named human reviewer with authority to stop [ ]; permitted tools [ ]; permitted synthetic inputs [ ]. Do not enter personal or confidential information into unapproved tools."}

{/*cf-review:field-512bb98225c14bf3b5a66cea3d86ae37*/"Proposed feedback tasks: Enter the supplied fictional garden-tidy request without coaching; change a detail on review; recover from a missing-field error; explain what the final screen means. Record any behaviour that must be simulated manually."}

{/*cf-review:field-4b3b85e9176c4a5b8c778daa66fbb690*/"Feedback record: Task completed [ ]; assistance needed [ ]; misunderstandings [ ]; suggested changes [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-7b04ee29997a4165ade274a93ebbbfb2*/"Time measures: Customer time per comparable task [ ]; owner review and correction time [ ]; combined handling time [ ]. Keep setup and revision time [ ] hours separate."}

{/*cf-review:field-db5bc86ba2bf4d84b876de099bc12cf6*/"Quality measures: Correct and complete tasks [ ] out of [ ]; critical errors [ ]; unresolved issues [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-6e771221d38149b2b86404d7990cafda*/"Actual spending: Tool expenses A$[ ]; participant expenses A$[ ]; other rehearsal expenses A$[ ]; total A$[ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-d2ad80a7b7864d2d8b8d391fc905035d*/"Continue threshold: For this hypothetical rehearsal, proceed only to a bounded design or feasibility test if time meets [target against baseline], quality meets [required successful tasks out of total], unresolved critical errors equal zero, and both caps are respected."}

{/*cf-review:field-01a77f85f5ea43e1a4d3f7c16af01cba*/"Revise threshold: Retest a fixable time or quality miss only if the proposed correction [ ] and retest fit within the remaining time and spending caps."}

{/*cf-review:field-08c024210dd04db3afc884ec59990bce*/"Stop or pause threshold: Stop or pause if a privacy or safety concern arises, a cap would be exceeded, or the agreed revision still fails the thresholds."}

{/*cf-review:field-75ab7e6c479043dab04ea0ef78ad192c*/"During the rehearsal, record what participants do and where they need help, rather than relying on whether they like the screens. If the owner manually rehearses receiving and assessing a request, label that handling as simulated. Do not count a simulated integration as working. Keep the customer's effort, the owner's effort and preparation time visible so that a quicker screen journey does not hide extra review work."}

{/*cf-review:field-e7f4cc599a7e4a30bf7f513ad149864c*/"No results or benchmark thresholds are supplied here. Rehearsal timings do not establish production savings, future operating costs or customer demand, and positive usability feedback does not authorise deployment."}

{/*cf-review:field-1e41ae7f42c04e7ea9d8d5f11b4443f6*/"Shortlist one use case and prepare your peer questions"}

{/*cf-review:field-c9c03f796c564503b4deb32f114bee7f*/"Write down your shortlisted use case as a hypothesis. For the hypothetical garden-maintenance business: \u201cExplore whether a three-screen quote-request flow helps prospective garden-tidy customers supply reviewable job details, with a person assessing every request.\u201d This remains an idea to test, not evidence of customer demand."}

{/*cf-review:field-98a4ae1532254986b40302db0a551e8b*/"Gather your prototype or preview, issue log and unrun pilot scorecard so a peer can see what you propose to test. Include an unresolved limitation, such as simulated rather than functioning field validation, and name the decision the rehearsal should inform: whether to continue to a bounded feasibility test, revise the design or stop. Peer experience can help identify gaps, but it does not replace intended-customer feedback, measured results or appropriate implementation review."}

{/*cf-review:field-ee390030ceab4bf4a4309885d5636f40*/"Explore MLAI events if you\u2019d like a peer conversation about your shortlisted use case and questions. Event availability, format and cost vary, so check the current listing and the organiser\u2019s details before deciding whether to attend."}

{/*cf-review:field-2d2d2b9df1f447fa8610d305e8e0350c*/"Attendance does not guarantee individual implementation advice. You can continue your bounded planning and feedback work without attending."}

{/*cf-review:field-732e4a1cb08548209030fff66fc2b5a3*/"Start with one customer task, not a whole product"}

{TOPIC} — {/*cf-review:field-e220b894cc114559a0dd75bedb470976*/"For a hypothetical first prototype, give an artificial intelligence design assistant one customer task and ask for three connected screens using fictional data. Inspect the generated copy and interactions yourself, then define a small, capped pilot before buying tools or commissioning development. Start with the business problem rather than the software, consistent with business.gov.au\u2019s guidance on introducing AI."}

{/*cf-review:field-6f548a46cb384cbb84eb1b5446f42523*/"Here, a design assistant means an AI tool you instruct to draft interface layouts, wording or screen specifications. Our hypothetical example is an Australian garden-maintenance business considering a quote-request option for one-off garden tidy-ups. No customer research, prototype testing or validation has been conducted for this example."}

{/*cf-review:field-ede08fb0808649828a1a7419e92e07ab*/"AI can help design that flow without being part of the eventual service. A person could still assess every quote request, and the finished form might not need AI at all. A clickable prototype does not establish readiness for live use, secure data handling, functioning integrations or customer demand."}

{/*cf-review:field-e6bfdcb676f14a4eaee3b364e0ed301d*/"Choose one problem and draw its boundaries"}

{/*cf-review:field-853ac952ec0042bc89b2e61f9e1ecf57*/"Business.gov.au recommends identifying the business problem first and looking at software you already use when considering solutions. Use this sentence to narrow your idea: \u201c[Customer] needs to [complete task] so that [specific outcome]; we will explore whether [proposed change] helps.\u201d The outcome should be something a person can review, rather than a promise that the tool will deliver a business result."}

{/*cf-review:field-884c1ba62fd84da29cf278c046668fe5*/"For the hypothetical garden-maintenance business: \u201cA prospective garden-tidy customer needs to provide enough job information for a person to assess a quote request; we will explore whether a guided request form helps.\u201d Assume the current alternative is a phone or email enquiry. Keep the proposed offering to a request for a one-off garden tidy-up, with a person deciding what happens next."}

{/*cf-review:field-2833da643d6e48198d126594a7b34928*/"In this hypothetical exercise, limit the demonstration to three primary screens: enter job details, review and edit those details, then view a clearly labelled simulated acknowledgement. Leave out payments, accounts, live availability, automatic prices and connections to customer-management systems. The final screen should say \u201cDemo only\u2014nothing has been sent\u201d to make its simulated status explicit. During the rehearsal, ask participants what that message means and record any misunderstanding about whether a request or booking was made."}

{/*cf-review:field-1b2f85c5749542449500b216a4255ae0*/"Before generating anything, check whether an existing business-approved tool supports editable screens, linked buttons and a preview. Confirm its current access, sharing, export and pricing restrictions rather than assuming these features are included. Record tool limitations before deciding whether another subscription is needed."}

{"Use synthetic inputs, and never enter personal or confidential information into an unapproved tool. Have a person review all generated copy and interactions before relying on them."}

{/*cf-review:field-c60f6cd8635b4219a03b0f95cf1663ac*/"Generate the screens and connect the flow"}

{/*cf-review:field-67e81da8dab1458db89ef792833479d8*/"Give the assistant the customer task, the information it can use, the output you want and the limits it must respect. OpenAI Academy\u2019s small-business workshop calls these Goal, Context, Output and Boundary. They help you explain the request without needing technical language. The hypothetical garden-tidy exercise below applies that structure; it does not assume your chosen tool can generate working, clickable screens."}

{/*cf-review:field-e8a8c252a1d247dd8b5d4c3ad56cb416*/"Check what the assistant actually returns. A screen specification describes the layout, words and behaviour. A static image shows an appearance but has no working controls. A clickable prototype connects screens so someone can follow a route. If the assistant supplies only copy, layouts, specifications or images, use them to assemble editable screens in an already-approved design or presentation tool."}

{/*cf-review:field-9dc957bc72aa48808309274b1e485a4d*/"Copy and adapt this prompt"}

{/*cf-review:field-6539bc71e95e4f4aa5c0a60dfa7505fb*/"Replace the bracketed descriptions with your intended business, customer and task. The supplied sample details belong to the hypothetical garden-tidy example and are synthetic, not customer records."}

{/*cf-review:field-53b702321abe4bd1af51832ca9e0bf3b*/"Act as a design assistant for [small business and proposed offering]. Intended user: [customer]. Task: [one customer task]. For this hypothetical exercise, create a low-fidelity, mobile-first prototype with exactly three primary screens: (1) enter the necessary details, (2) review them and edit, and (3) view a simulated acknowledgement. Keep the layout simple and suitable for a narrow phone screen."}

{/*cf-review:field-8a7785c7c26c4b6c9915a3d9af930fa0*/"For this hypothetical garden-tidy example, use only these synthetic details: Sample Customer A; demo@example.com; service: one-off garden tidy; garden size: small; job note: weed beds and sweep paths. Include labelled fields, concise plain-English copy, a missing-required-field state and an invalid-email state within the relevant screen. Specify forward, edit/back and restart interactions. Use readable text and errors that do not rely on colour alone."}

{/*cf-review:field-8372339b701141e290bc273c92dc2715*/"Do not create real accounts, send messages, store submissions, connect services, quote prices or promise availability. Label the final screen: Demo only\u2014nothing has been sent. Output editable screens and an interaction map if supported; otherwise provide a screen specification and exact linking instructions. List assumptions, simulated behaviours and anything requiring human review. Do not invent customer findings."}

{/*cf-review:field-69c940251cf64bacb1cd4b416d11f7fe*/"Connect the screens and check the preview"}

{/*cf-review:field-f856acf6cc704cea84196c3564710be2*/"For the hypothetical garden-tidy flow, link the job-details screen to the review screen. From review, provide an edit action that returns to job details and a simulated submission action that opens the acknowledgement. Let the acknowledgement restart the demonstration. If the tool has not created those links, connect the buttons manually where supported, then follow each route in preview or presentation mode."}

{/*cf-review:field-74c4d5f21093458384443e3d0bfb3de2*/"Links alone do not prove that form behaviour works. If the prototype cannot accept typed details, label that behaviour as simulated and record the limitation."}

{/*cf-review:field-bbb3c16921e54adea53003f7a5063ec3*/"Walk through the prototype before showing it to anyone"}

{/*cf-review:field-b8187ffde3534eafa885171d6d3d0957*/"Inspect the generated screens yourself rather than accepting the assistant\u2019s claim that they work. Business.gov.au advises checking AI-generated information before relying on it. For this hypothetical garden-tidy prototype, start with the normal route using the supplied synthetic details: enter the request, review it and open the simulated acknowledgement. Check that necessary details are requested before review, the review matches the input and every button reaches its intended destination."}

{/*cf-review:field-1952efe8ae464f70b94be2bbf9f59dbb*/"Then try the correction routes. Leave a required field blank, enter an invalid fictional email address, return from review to change the garden size, then restart the demonstration. Keep a short issue log recording the route, expected behaviour, observed behaviour and anything you simulated manually. A drawn error message does not demonstrate functioning validation. If the prototype cannot preserve edited values or respond to invalid input, record that limitation rather than treating the route as passed."}

{/*cf-review:field-4be734afddd847c892146afc9bcd6d54*/"Read the copy alongside those interactions. Look for unexplained fields, missing instructions and promises about prices, availability or messages being sent that the demonstration cannot fulfil. Where \u201cContinue\u201d leaves the destination unclear, use a label such as \u201cReview job details\u201d. Check that the acknowledgement describes a simulation, not a real quote request or booking, and that returning to edit is easy to find."}

{/*cf-review:field-2d63f3610f5a4c55a6f5a343369ef7bc*/"Open a narrow mobile preview and inspect it for clipped content, readable text and enough spacing to distinguish adjacent buttons. Where the tool permits, try keyboard navigation and zoom, and check whether keyboard focus remains visible. Inspect field labels and make sure errors explain the problem in words rather than relying on colour alone. Mark checks the tool cannot support as \u201cnot testable here\u201d. These are practical checks for this exercise, not a comprehensive accessibility audit, security assessment or proof of operational reliability."}

{/*cf-review:field-7ff25ec5353b47bda0ecf5562d8a1b7c*/"Ask for a bounded revision, then repeat the affected route. For example, in this hypothetical prototype: \u201cOn the review screen, add an Edit job details action that returns to the entry screen; keep all other copy unchanged.\u201d Check the revised copy and links yourself, and update the issue log with what changed, what remains unresolved and what is still simulated."}

{/*cf-review:field-f5fabdfa8e1447659331d3b193f31ff8*/"Draft a capped pilot before committing money"}

{/*cf-review:field-c46d85d2a8844c9c9762073acf87cd64*/"Plan a usability rehearsal with synthetic information, not a live quote-request service. For the hypothetical garden-tidy offering, invite willing participants who resemble the intended customer where feasible, explain that nothing will be submitted, and name a human reviewer who can check outputs and stop the exercise. The immediate question is whether people can complete and understand the proposed flow, not whether the business is ready to launch it."}

{/*cf-review:field-8e1e20ac0f924c5a907364e03db448a7*/"Set the time and spending limits before inviting participants or buying tools. Record a comparable baseline for the current enquiry process, including customer effort and the owner's checking and correction work. MLAI's workflow-selection guide recommends observing the existing process and separating setup from recurring effort. If you have no comparable baseline, write \u201cnot measured\u201d and collect it before claiming an improvement."}

{/*cf-review:field-413fc18402654e56b13082815fde80c9*/"Fill in the pilot scorecard"}

{/*cf-review:field-892349cbbedd42869aa24587505fc7b4*/"Copy this scorecard and fill in the plan before running the rehearsal. The tasks and decision rules below are a planning exercise for the hypothetical garden-tidy example, not a validated assessment method. Set your own thresholds against the baseline and the limits your business can afford."}

{/*cf-review:field-d996ef4b80fc4d04b1a7c6fa16e738a5*/"Current workflow and comparison: Current workflow [ ]; comparable task or scenario [ ]; observation period or rehearsal count [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-e824e1a769284adb92f8ec54f06541f0*/"Baseline measures: Customer completion time [ ]; owner review and correction time [ ]; complete and accurate requests [ ] out of [ ]. Record \u201cnot measured\u201d wherever evidence is missing."}

{/*cf-review:field-b5a5a07276bc44969e31a9a9cddabb81*/"Scope and dates: Shortlisted use case [ ]; start date [ ]; review date [ ]; participant count [ ]; task count [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-ae57d39ce0ad43ad8ee53319260b0c5d*/"Time and spending caps: Total setup, testing and revision cap [ ] hours; cash spending cap A$[ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-8868f83fe35d428898586ece4a391e5b*/"Responsibility and data boundary: Named human reviewer with authority to stop [ ]; permitted tools [ ]; permitted synthetic inputs [ ]. Do not enter personal or confidential information into unapproved tools."}

{/*cf-review:field-512bb98225c14bf3b5a66cea3d86ae37*/"Proposed feedback tasks: Enter the supplied fictional garden-tidy request without coaching; change a detail on review; recover from a missing-field error; explain what the final screen means. Record any behaviour that must be simulated manually."}

{/*cf-review:field-4b3b85e9176c4a5b8c778daa66fbb690*/"Feedback record: Task completed [ ]; assistance needed [ ]; misunderstandings [ ]; suggested changes [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-7b04ee29997a4165ade274a93ebbbfb2*/"Time measures: Customer time per comparable task [ ]; owner review and correction time [ ]; combined handling time [ ]. Keep setup and revision time [ ] hours separate."}

{/*cf-review:field-db5bc86ba2bf4d84b876de099bc12cf6*/"Quality measures: Correct and complete tasks [ ] out of [ ]; critical errors [ ]; unresolved issues [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-6e771221d38149b2b86404d7990cafda*/"Actual spending: Tool expenses A$[ ]; participant expenses A$[ ]; other rehearsal expenses A$[ ]; total A$[ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-d2ad80a7b7864d2d8b8d391fc905035d*/"Continue threshold: For this hypothetical rehearsal, proceed only to a bounded design or feasibility test if time meets [target against baseline], quality meets [required successful tasks out of total], unresolved critical errors equal zero, and both caps are respected."}

{/*cf-review:field-01a77f85f5ea43e1a4d3f7c16af01cba*/"Revise threshold: Retest a fixable time or quality miss only if the proposed correction [ ] and retest fit within the remaining time and spending caps."}

{/*cf-review:field-08c024210dd04db3afc884ec59990bce*/"Stop or pause threshold: Stop or pause if a privacy or safety concern arises, a cap would be exceeded, or the agreed revision still fails the thresholds."}

{/*cf-review:field-75ab7e6c479043dab04ea0ef78ad192c*/"During the rehearsal, record what participants do and where they need help, rather than relying on whether they like the screens. If the owner manually rehearses receiving and assessing a request, label that handling as simulated. Do not count a simulated integration as working. Keep the customer's effort, the owner's effort and preparation time visible so that a quicker screen journey does not hide extra review work."}

{/*cf-review:field-e7f4cc599a7e4a30bf7f513ad149864c*/"No results or benchmark thresholds are supplied here. Rehearsal timings do not establish production savings, future operating costs or customer demand, and positive usability feedback does not authorise deployment."}

{/*cf-review:field-1e41ae7f42c04e7ea9d8d5f11b4443f6*/"Shortlist one use case and prepare your peer questions"}

{/*cf-review:field-732e4a1cb08548209030fff66fc2b5a3*/"Start with one customer task, not a whole product"}

{TOPIC} — {/*cf-review:field-e220b894cc114559a0dd75bedb470976*/"For a hypothetical first prototype, give an artificial intelligence design assistant one customer task and ask for three connected screens using fictional data. Inspect the generated copy and interactions yourself, then define a small, capped pilot before buying tools or commissioning development. Start with the business problem rather than the software, consistent with business.gov.au\u2019s guidance on introducing AI."}

{/*cf-review:field-6f548a46cb384cbb84eb1b5446f42523*/"Here, a design assistant means an AI tool you instruct to draft interface layouts, wording or screen specifications. Our hypothetical example is an Australian garden-maintenance business considering a quote-request option for one-off garden tidy-ups. No customer research, prototype testing or validation has been conducted for this example."}

{/*cf-review:field-ede08fb0808649828a1a7419e92e07ab*/"AI can help design that flow without being part of the eventual service. A person could still assess every quote request, and the finished form might not need AI at all. A clickable prototype does not establish readiness for live use, secure data handling, functioning integrations or customer demand."}

{/*cf-review:field-e6bfdcb676f14a4eaee3b364e0ed301d*/"Choose one problem and draw its boundaries"}

{/*cf-review:field-853ac952ec0042bc89b2e61f9e1ecf57*/"Business.gov.au recommends identifying the business problem first and looking at software you already use when considering solutions. Use this sentence to narrow your idea: \u201c[Customer] needs to [complete task] so that [specific outcome]; we will explore whether [proposed change] helps.\u201d The outcome should be something a person can review, rather than a promise that the tool will deliver a business result."}

{/*cf-review:field-884c1ba62fd84da29cf278c046668fe5*/"For the hypothetical garden-maintenance business: \u201cA prospective garden-tidy customer needs to provide enough job information for a person to assess a quote request; we will explore whether a guided request form helps.\u201d Assume the current alternative is a phone or email enquiry. Keep the proposed offering to a request for a one-off garden tidy-up, with a person deciding what happens next."}

{/*cf-review:field-2833da643d6e48198d126594a7b34928*/"In this hypothetical exercise, limit the demonstration to three primary screens: enter job details, review and edit those details, then view a clearly labelled simulated acknowledgement. Leave out payments, accounts, live availability, automatic prices and connections to customer-management systems. The final screen should say \u201cDemo only\u2014nothing has been sent\u201d to make its simulated status explicit. During the rehearsal, ask participants what that message means and record any misunderstanding about whether a request or booking was made."}

{/*cf-review:field-1b2f85c5749542449500b216a4255ae0*/"Before generating anything, check whether an existing business-approved tool supports editable screens, linked buttons and a preview. Confirm its current access, sharing, export and pricing restrictions rather than assuming these features are included. Record tool limitations before deciding whether another subscription is needed."}

{"Use synthetic inputs, and never enter personal or confidential information into an unapproved tool. Have a person review all generated copy and interactions before relying on them."}

{/*cf-review:field-c60f6cd8635b4219a03b0f95cf1663ac*/"Generate the screens and connect the flow"}

{/*cf-review:field-67e81da8dab1458db89ef792833479d8*/"Give the assistant the customer task, the information it can use, the output you want and the limits it must respect. OpenAI Academy\u2019s small-business workshop calls these Goal, Context, Output and Boundary. They help you explain the request without needing technical language. The hypothetical garden-tidy exercise below applies that structure; it does not assume your chosen tool can generate working, clickable screens."}

{/*cf-review:field-e8a8c252a1d247dd8b5d4c3ad56cb416*/"Check what the assistant actually returns. A screen specification describes the layout, words and behaviour. A static image shows an appearance but has no working controls. A clickable prototype connects screens so someone can follow a route. If the assistant supplies only copy, layouts, specifications or images, use them to assemble editable screens in an already-approved design or presentation tool."}

{/*cf-review:field-9dc957bc72aa48808309274b1e485a4d*/"Copy and adapt this prompt"}

{/*cf-review:field-6539bc71e95e4f4aa5c0a60dfa7505fb*/"Replace the bracketed descriptions with your intended business, customer and task. The supplied sample details belong to the hypothetical garden-tidy example and are synthetic, not customer records."}

{/*cf-review:field-53b702321abe4bd1af51832ca9e0bf3b*/"Act as a design assistant for [small business and proposed offering]. Intended user: [customer]. Task: [one customer task]. For this hypothetical exercise, create a low-fidelity, mobile-first prototype with exactly three primary screens: (1) enter the necessary details, (2) review them and edit, and (3) view a simulated acknowledgement. Keep the layout simple and suitable for a narrow phone screen."}

{/*cf-review:field-8a7785c7c26c4b6c9915a3d9af930fa0*/"For this hypothetical garden-tidy example, use only these synthetic details: Sample Customer A; demo@example.com; service: one-off garden tidy; garden size: small; job note: weed beds and sweep paths. Include labelled fields, concise plain-English copy, a missing-required-field state and an invalid-email state within the relevant screen. Specify forward, edit/back and restart interactions. Use readable text and errors that do not rely on colour alone."}

{/*cf-review:field-8372339b701141e290bc273c92dc2715*/"Do not create real accounts, send messages, store submissions, connect services, quote prices or promise availability. Label the final screen: Demo only\u2014nothing has been sent. Output editable screens and an interaction map if supported; otherwise provide a screen specification and exact linking instructions. List assumptions, simulated behaviours and anything requiring human review. Do not invent customer findings."}

{/*cf-review:field-69c940251cf64bacb1cd4b416d11f7fe*/"Connect the screens and check the preview"}

{/*cf-review:field-f856acf6cc704cea84196c3564710be2*/"For the hypothetical garden-tidy flow, link the job-details screen to the review screen. From review, provide an edit action that returns to job details and a simulated submission action that opens the acknowledgement. Let the acknowledgement restart the demonstration. If the tool has not created those links, connect the buttons manually where supported, then follow each route in preview or presentation mode."}

{/*cf-review:field-74c4d5f21093458384443e3d0bfb3de2*/"Links alone do not prove that form behaviour works. If the prototype cannot accept typed details, label that behaviour as simulated and record the limitation."}

{/*cf-review:field-bbb3c16921e54adea53003f7a5063ec3*/"Walk through the prototype before showing it to anyone"}

{/*cf-review:field-b8187ffde3534eafa885171d6d3d0957*/"Inspect the generated screens yourself rather than accepting the assistant\u2019s claim that they work. Business.gov.au advises checking AI-generated information before relying on it. For this hypothetical garden-tidy prototype, start with the normal route using the supplied synthetic details: enter the request, review it and open the simulated acknowledgement. Check that necessary details are requested before review, the review matches the input and every button reaches its intended destination."}

{/*cf-review:field-1952efe8ae464f70b94be2bbf9f59dbb*/"Then try the correction routes. Leave a required field blank, enter an invalid fictional email address, return from review to change the garden size, then restart the demonstration. Keep a short issue log recording the route, expected behaviour, observed behaviour and anything you simulated manually. A drawn error message does not demonstrate functioning validation. If the prototype cannot preserve edited values or respond to invalid input, record that limitation rather than treating the route as passed."}

{/*cf-review:field-4be734afddd847c892146afc9bcd6d54*/"Read the copy alongside those interactions. Look for unexplained fields, missing instructions and promises about prices, availability or messages being sent that the demonstration cannot fulfil. Where \u201cContinue\u201d leaves the destination unclear, use a label such as \u201cReview job details\u201d. Check that the acknowledgement describes a simulation, not a real quote request or booking, and that returning to edit is easy to find."}

{/*cf-review:field-2d63f3610f5a4c55a6f5a343369ef7bc*/"Open a narrow mobile preview and inspect it for clipped content, readable text and enough spacing to distinguish adjacent buttons. Where the tool permits, try keyboard navigation and zoom, and check whether keyboard focus remains visible. Inspect field labels and make sure errors explain the problem in words rather than relying on colour alone. Mark checks the tool cannot support as \u201cnot testable here\u201d. These are practical checks for this exercise, not a comprehensive accessibility audit, security assessment or proof of operational reliability."}

{/*cf-review:field-7ff25ec5353b47bda0ecf5562d8a1b7c*/"Ask for a bounded revision, then repeat the affected route. For example, in this hypothetical prototype: \u201cOn the review screen, add an Edit job details action that returns to the entry screen; keep all other copy unchanged.\u201d Check the revised copy and links yourself, and update the issue log with what changed, what remains unresolved and what is still simulated."}

{/*cf-review:field-f5fabdfa8e1447659331d3b193f31ff8*/"Draft a capped pilot before committing money"}

{/*cf-review:field-c46d85d2a8844c9c9762073acf87cd64*/"Plan a usability rehearsal with synthetic information, not a live quote-request service. For the hypothetical garden-tidy offering, invite willing participants who resemble the intended customer where feasible, explain that nothing will be submitted, and name a human reviewer who can check outputs and stop the exercise. The immediate question is whether people can complete and understand the proposed flow, not whether the business is ready to launch it."}

{/*cf-review:field-8e1e20ac0f924c5a907364e03db448a7*/"Set the time and spending limits before inviting participants or buying tools. Record a comparable baseline for the current enquiry process, including customer effort and the owner's checking and correction work. MLAI's workflow-selection guide recommends observing the existing process and separating setup from recurring effort. If you have no comparable baseline, write \u201cnot measured\u201d and collect it before claiming an improvement."}

{/*cf-review:field-413fc18402654e56b13082815fde80c9*/"Fill in the pilot scorecard"}

{/*cf-review:field-892349cbbedd42869aa24587505fc7b4*/"Copy this scorecard and fill in the plan before running the rehearsal. The tasks and decision rules below are a planning exercise for the hypothetical garden-tidy example, not a validated assessment method. Set your own thresholds against the baseline and the limits your business can afford."}

{/*cf-review:field-d996ef4b80fc4d04b1a7c6fa16e738a5*/"Current workflow and comparison: Current workflow [ ]; comparable task or scenario [ ]; observation period or rehearsal count [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-e824e1a769284adb92f8ec54f06541f0*/"Baseline measures: Customer completion time [ ]; owner review and correction time [ ]; complete and accurate requests [ ] out of [ ]. Record \u201cnot measured\u201d wherever evidence is missing."}

{/*cf-review:field-b5a5a07276bc44969e31a9a9cddabb81*/"Scope and dates: Shortlisted use case [ ]; start date [ ]; review date [ ]; participant count [ ]; task count [ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-ae57d39ce0ad43ad8ee53319260b0c5d*/"Time and spending caps: Total setup, testing and revision cap [ ] hours; cash spending cap A$[ ]."}

{/*cf-review:field-8868f83fe35d428898586ece4a391e5b*/"Responsibility and data boundary: Named human reviewer with authority to stop [ ]; permitted tools [ ]; permitted synthetic inputs [ ]. Do not enter personal or confidential information into unapproved tools."}

{/*cf-review:field-512bb98225c14bf3b5a66cea3d86ae37*/"Proposed feedback tasks: Enter the supplied fictional garden-tidy request without coaching; change a detail on review; recover from a missing-field error; explain what the final screen means. Record any behaviour that must be simulated manually."}

{/*cf-review:field-4b3b85e9176c4a5b8c778daa66fbb690*/"Feedback record: Task completed [ ]; assistance needed [ ]; misunderstandings [ ]; suggested changes [ ]."}

editorial_brief.reader_task: Use an AI design assistant to turn one startup idea into a low-cost, clickable prototype of a customer workflow, then draft a small pilot plan before buying tools or commissioning development.
editorial_brief.distinct_contribution: Provide a beginner-friendly, tool-neutral walkthrough for an Australian small business owner exploring a new offering: narrow the idea to one customer task, generate a three-screen prototype using synthetic data, check its interactions manually, and prepare a pilot scorecard. Clearly distinguish using AI to design a prototype from building a working AI-powered product.
acceptance_criteria: Frame the startup idea as a new small-business offering with one bounded customer problem, rather than a venture-scale product build.
Use one explicitly hypothetical example throughout, such as a quote-request workflow for a small service business; do not imply that research, testing or customer validation has already occurred.
Include a reusable design-assistant prompt specifying the intended user, task, three-screen flow, constraints, synthetic sample data and desired output.
Explain how to inspect and revise the generated screens for missing steps, unclear copy, error states, accessibility basics and mobile usability.
State that a clickable prototype does not establish production readiness, secure data handling, functioning integrations or customer demand.

Include a fill-in pilot plan covering the current workflow baseline, time and spending caps, human reviewer, proposed feedback tasks, and time, quality and cost measures with continue, revise or stop thresholds.
Warn readers not to enter confidential or personal information into unapproved tools, and require human review of generated outputs.
End the practical workflow with one shortlisted use case and questions to ask peers about feasibility, tool limitations and pilot measurement.

Keep the business next action separate from the reader task: offer the optional 'Explore MLAI events' CTA linking to '/events' only after the use case and peer questions are drafted. Explain that event availability, format and cost vary and attendance does not guarantee individual implementation advice.

package.article_markdown: # Use an Artificial Intelligence Design Assistant to Prototype Prototype a hypothetical small-business workflow with synthetic data, check its interactions and plan a capped pilot before paying for development. ![Two people look at a laptop at a table. One points toward it while the other, wearing glasses, rests a hand against their chin.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU05QPB483K9%2FMLAI-AUS-Inc%2Fmlai-au%2Fimages%2Fhero-6f255f22-52be-4e14-a162-6ea7c04e7054.jpg?alt=media&token=f8e00c6f-f254-425a-ab00-293e2c007690) *Prototype a hypothetical small-business workflow with synthetic data, check its interactions and plan a capped pilot before paying for development.* ## Quick Summary - **What can an artificial intelligence design assistant produce?:** Some AI design tools generate editable interface layouts from text prompts and provide text-generation features for interface copy. Check whether buttons actually connect screens before treating the output as a clickable prototype. - **How can you prototype a small-business idea?:** For a hypothetical garden-tidy offering, connect three screens: job details, review and edit, and a simulated acknowledgement. Use synthetic data and manually check navigation, error states and mobile readability. - **What should a prototype pilot measure?:** Measure task time, completeness, errors and spending against a comparable baseline. Record customer effort, owner review and setup separately, with time and spending caps and agreed continue, revise or stop thresholds. ## Start with one customer task, not a whole product For a hypothetical first prototype, give an artificial intelligence design assistant one customer task and ask for three connected screens using fictional data. Inspect the generated copy and interactions yourself, then define a small, capped pilot before buying tools or commissioning development. Start with the business problem rather than the software, consistent with business.gov.au’s guidance on introducing AI. Here, a design assistant means an AI tool you instruct to draft interface layouts, wording or screen specifications. Our hypothetical example is an Australian garden-maintenance business considering a quote-request option for one-off garden tidy-ups. No customer research, prototype testing or validation has been conducted for this example. AI can help design that flow without being part of the eventual service. A person could still assess every quote request, and the finished form might not need AI at all. A clickable prototype does not establish readiness for live use, secure data handling, functioning integrations or customer demand. ## Choose one problem and draw its boundaries Business.gov.au recommends identifying the business problem first and looking at software you already use when considering solutions. Use this sentence to narrow your idea: “[Customer] needs to [complete task] so that [specific outcome]; we will explore whether [proposed change] helps.” The outcome should be something a person can review, rather than a promise that the tool will deliver a business result. For the hypothetical garden-maintenance business: “A prospective garden-tidy customer needs to provide enough job information for a person to assess a quote request; we will explore whether a guided request form helps.” Assume the current alternative is a phone or email enquiry. Keep the proposed offering to a request for a one-off garden tidy-up, with a person deciding what happens next. In this hypothetical exercise, limit the demonstration to three primary screens: enter job details, review and edit those details, then view a clearly labelled simulated acknowledgement. Leave out payments, accounts, live availability, automatic prices and connections to customer-management systems. The final screen should say “Demo only—nothing has been sent” to make its simulated status explicit. During the rehearsal, ask participants what that message means and record any misunderstanding about whether a request or booking was made. Before generating anything, check whether an existing business-approved tool supports editable screens, linked buttons and a preview. Confirm its current access, sharing, export and pricing restrictions rather than assuming these features are included. Record tool limitations before deciding whether another subscription is needed. ![A hand draws a garden layout in a notebook on a weathered wooden table beside gardening gloves, a mug, and a potted plant.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU05QPB483K9%2FMLAI-AUS-Inc%2Fmlai-au%2Fimages%2Finline-6ca837ad-c141-4a9e-84ac-b5f7a088507c.jpg?alt=media&token=52e98946-b132-4b80-9342-263bc4231c8d) > ### Keep real customer data out > > Use synthetic inputs, and never enter personal or confidential information into an unapproved tool. Have a person review all generated copy and interactions before relying on them. ## Generate the screens and connect the flow Give the assistant the customer task, the information it can use, the output you want and the limits it must respect. OpenAI Academy’s small-business workshop calls these Goal, Context, Output and Boundary. They help you explain the request without needing technical language. The hypothetical garden-tidy exercise below applies that structure; it does not assume your chosen tool can generate working, clickable screens. Check what the assistant actually returns. A screen specification describes the layout, words and behaviour. A static image shows an appearance but has no working controls. A clickable prototype connects screens so someone can follow a route. If the assistant supplies only copy, layouts, specifications or images, use them to assemble editable screens in an already-approved design or presentation tool. ### Copy and adapt this prompt Replace the bracketed descriptions with your intended business, customer and task. The supplied sample details belong to the hypothetical garden-tidy example and are synthetic, not customer records. Act as a design assistant for [small business and proposed offering]. Intended user: [customer]. Task: [one customer task]. For this hypothetical exercise, create a low-fidelity, mobile-first prototype with exactly three primary screens: (1) enter the necessary details, (2) review them and edit, and (3) view a simulated acknowledgement. Keep the layout simple and suitable for a narrow phone screen. For this hypothetical garden-tidy example, use only these synthetic details: Sample Customer A; demo@example.com; service: one-off garden tidy; garden size: small; job note: weed beds and sweep paths. Include labelled fields, concise plain-English copy, a missing-required-field state and an invalid-email state within the relevant screen. Specify forward, edit/back and restart interactions. Use readable text and errors that do not rely on colour alone. Do not create real accounts, send messages, store submissions, connect services, quote prices or promise availability. Label the final screen: Demo only—nothing has been sent. Output editable screens and an interaction map if supported; otherwise provide a screen specification and exact linking instructions. List assumptions, simulated behaviours and anything requiring human review. Do not invent customer findings. ### Connect the screens and check the preview For the hypothetical garden-tidy flow, link the job-details screen to the review screen. From review, provide an edit action that returns to job details and a simulated submission action that opens the acknowledgement. Let the acknowledgement restart the demonstration. If the tool has not created those links, connect the buttons manually where supported, then follow each route in preview or presentation mode. Links alone do not prove that form behaviour works. If the prototype cannot accept typed details, label that behaviour as simulated and record the limitation. ## Walk through the prototype before showing it to anyone Inspect the generated screens yourself rather than accepting the assistant’s claim that they work. Business.gov.au advises checking AI-generated information before relying on it. For this hypothetical garden-tidy prototype, start with the normal route using the supplied synthetic details: enter the request, review it and open the simulated acknowledgement. Check that necessary details are requested before review, the review matches the input and every button reaches its intended destination. Then try the correction routes. Leave a required field blank, enter an invalid fictional email address, return from review to change the garden size, then restart the demonstration. Keep a short issue log recording the route, expected behaviour, observed behaviour and anything you simulated manually. A drawn error message does not demonstrate functioning validation. If the prototype cannot preserve edited values or respond to invalid input, record that limitation rather than treating the route as passed. Read the copy alongside those interactions. Look for unexplained fields, missing instructions and promises about prices, availability or messages being sent that the demonstration cannot fulfil. Where “Continue” leaves the destination unclear, use a label such as “Review job details”. Check that the acknowledgement describes a simulation, not a real quote request or booking, and that returning to edit is easy to find. Open a narrow mobile preview and inspect it for clipped content, readable text and enough spacing to distinguish adjacent buttons. Where the tool permits, try keyboard navigation and zoom, and check whether keyboard focus remains visible. Inspect field labels and make sure errors explain the problem in words rather than relying on colour alone. Mark checks the tool cannot support as “not testable here”. These are practical checks for this exercise, not a comprehensive accessibility audit, security assessment or proof of operational reliability. Ask for a bounded revision, then repeat the affected route. For example, in this hypothetical prototype: “On the review screen, add an Edit job details action that returns to the entry screen; keep all other copy unchanged.” Check the revised copy and links yourself, and update the issue log with what changed, what remains unresolved and what is still simulated. ![An open laptop, mug, notebook and pen sit on a wooden garden table beside a potted plant, with greenery in the background.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU05QPB483K9%2FMLAI-AUS-Inc%2Fmlai-au%2Fimages%2Finline-bbd5f133-5723-443a-8776-d93638e8b712.jpg?alt=media&token=42bb4603-36ea-40ca-a4e3-cd414404f49d) ## Draft a capped pilot before committing money Plan a usability rehearsal with synthetic information, not a live quote-request service. For the hypothetical garden-tidy offering, invite willing participants who resemble the intended customer where feasible, explain that nothing will be submitted, and name a human reviewer who can check outputs and stop the exercise. The immediate question is whether people can complete and understand the proposed flow, not whether the business is ready to launch it. Set the time and spending limits before inviting participants or buying tools. Record a comparable baseline for the current enquiry process, including customer effort and the owner's checking and correction work. MLAI's workflow-selection guide recommends observing the existing process and separating setup from recurring effort. If you have no comparable baseline, write “not measured” and collect it before claiming an improvement. ### Fill in the pilot scorecard Copy this scorecard and fill in the plan before running the rehearsal. The tasks and decision rules below are a planning exercise for the hypothetical garden-tidy example, not a validated assessment method. Set your own thresholds against the baseline and the limits your business can afford. Current workflow and comparison: Current workflow [ ]; comparable task or scenario [ ]; observation period or rehearsal count [ ]. Baseline measures: Customer completion time [ ]; owner review and correction time [ ]; complete and accurate requests [ ] out of [ ]. Record “not measured” wherever evidence is missing. Scope and dates: Shortlisted use case [ ]; start date [ ]; review date [ ]; participant count [ ]; task count [ ]. Time and spending caps: Total setup, testing and revision cap [ ] hours; cash spending cap A$[ ]. Responsibility and data boundary: Named human reviewer with authority to stop [ ]; permitted tools [ ]; permitted synthetic inputs [ ]. Do not enter personal or confidential information into unapproved tools. Proposed feedback tasks: Enter the supplied fictional garden-tidy request without coaching; change a detail on review; recover from a missing-field error; explain what the final screen means. Record any behaviour that must be simulated manually. Feedback record: Task completed [ ]; assistance needed [ ]; misunderstandings [ ]; suggested changes [ ]. Time measures: Customer time per comparable task [ ]; owner review and correction time [ ]; combined handling time [ ]. Keep setup and revision time [ ] hours separate. Quality measures: Correct and complete tasks [ ] out of [ ]; critical errors [ ]; unresolved issues [ ]. Actual spending: Tool expenses A$[ ]; participant expenses A$[ ]; other rehearsal expenses A$[ ]; total A$[ ]. Continue threshold: For this hypothetical rehearsal, proceed only to a bounded design or feasibility test if time meets [target against baseline], quality meets [required successful tasks out of total], unresolved critical errors equal zero, and both caps are respected. Revise threshold: Retest a fixable time or quality miss only if the proposed correction [ ] and retest fit within the remaining time and spending caps. Stop or pause threshold: Stop or pause if a privacy or safety concern arises, a cap would be exceeded, or the agreed revision still fails the thresholds. During the rehearsal, record what participants do and where they need help, rather than relying on whether they like the screens. If the owner manually rehearses receiving and assessing a request, label that handling as simulated. Do not count a simulated integration as working. Keep the customer's effort, the owner's effort and preparation time visible so that a quicker screen journey does not hide extra review work. No results or benchmark thresholds are supplied here. Rehearsal timings do not establish production savings, future operating costs or customer demand, and positive usability feedback does not authorise deployment. ![Close-up of two people looking down at a notebook, with a hand holding a pen in the foreground.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU05QPB483K9%2FMLAI-AUS-Inc%2Fmlai-au%2Fimages%2Finline-c6b7f3fb-9788-4f29-a48e-abcc6923e50f.jpg?alt=media&token=7b45fca0-5aaa-4a50-a9e4-af09591b7405) ## Shortlist one use case and prepare your peer questions Write down your shortlisted use case as a hypothesis. For the hypothetical garden-maintenance business: “Explore whether a three-screen quote-request flow helps prospective garden-tidy customers supply reviewable job details, with a person assessing every request.” This remains an idea to test, not evidence of customer demand. Gather your prototype or preview, issue log and unrun pilot scorecard so a peer can see what you propose to test. Include an unresolved limitation, such as simulated rather than functioning field validation, and name the decision the rehearsal should inform: whether to continue to a bounded feasibility test, revise the design or stop. Peer experience can help identify gaps, but it does not replace intended-customer feedback, measured results or appropriate implementation review. - What would have to work beyond these screens before this flow could be used for real requests? - Which editing, validation, mobile, sharing or export limitations should I check in my current tools? - Are my baseline, task count, review-time accounting and continue, revise or stop thresholds useful for this small rehearsal? ## Optional next step for a peer conversation Explore MLAI events if you’d like a peer conversation about your shortlisted use case and questions. Event availability, format and cost vary, so check the current listing and the organiser’s details before deciding whether to attend. Attendance does not guarantee individual implementation advice. You can continue your bounded planning and feedback work without attending. ![Four people sit around a low table as one gestures. A mug, bottle and plant sit on the table, with more people and a whiteboard behind.](https://firebasestorage.googleapis.com/v0/b/mlai-main-website.firebasestorage.app/o/content-factory%2FU05QPB483K9%2FMLAI-AUS-Inc%2Fmlai-au%2Fimages%2Finline-72dc8a1a-2afe-4bee-b749-c7b13ca78102.jpg?alt=media&token=a39c4ef8-3e3d-43b4-baab-40267c58eada) ## Next Step **Get in touch about MLAI Studio** Browse testimonials and case studies from MLAI Studio, understand how MLAI Studio works, the price per month and how many builder hours that buys you. [Explore MLAI Studio](https://mlai.au/mlai-studio) ## References - [Artificial intelligence (AI) | business.gov.au](https://business.gov.au/online-and-digital/artificial-intelligence) - [ChatGPT for Small Business | Workshop Resource Hub - Resource | OpenAI Academy](https://academy.openai.com/public/resources/openai-academy-small-business-resource-hub-2026-06-03) - [Getting started with AI: choose one business workflow | MLAI](https://mlai.au/articles/featured/how-to-get-started-with-ai-2026) - [Uizard's AI-powered Design Assistant | Uizard](https://uizard.io/design-assistant/)

sections.heading: Start with one customer task, not a whole product
paragraphs: For a hypothetical first prototype, give an artificial intelligence design assistant one customer task and ask for three connected screens using fictional data. Inspect the generated copy and interactions yourself, then define a small, capped pilot before buying tools or commissioning development. Start with the business problem rather than the software, consistent with business.gov.au’s guidance on introducing AI.

Here, a design assistant means an AI tool you instruct to draft interface layouts, wording or screen specifications. Our hypothetical example is an Australian garden-maintenance business considering a quote-request option for one-off garden tidy-ups. No customer research, prototype testing or validation has been conducted for this example.

AI can help design that flow without being part of the eventual service. A person could still assess every quote request, and the finished form might not need AI at all. A clickable prototype does not establish readiness for live use, secure data handling, functioning integrations or customer demand.

sections.heading: Choose one problem and draw its boundaries
paragraphs: Business.gov.au recommends identifying the business problem first and looking at software you already use when considering solutions. Use this sentence to narrow your idea: “[Customer] needs to [complete task] so that [specific outcome]; we will explore whether [proposed change] helps.” The outcome should be something a person can review, rather than a promise that the tool will deliver a business result.

For the hypothetical garden-maintenance business: “A prospective garden-tidy customer needs to provide enough job information for a person to assess a quote request; we will explore whether a guided request form helps.” Assume the current alternative is a phone or email enquiry. Keep the proposed offering to a request for a one-off garden tidy-up, with a person deciding what happens next.

In this hypothetical exercise, limit the demonstration to three primary screens: enter job details, review and edit those details, then view a clearly labelled simulated acknowledgement. Leave out payments, accounts, live availability, automatic prices and connections to customer-management systems. The final screen should say “Demo only—nothing has been sent” to make its simulated status explicit. During the rehearsal, ask participants what that message means and record any misunderstanding about whether a request or booking was made.

Before generating anything, check whether an existing business-approved tool supports editable screens, linked buttons and a preview. Confirm its current access, sharing, export and pricing restrictions rather than assuming these features are included. Record tool limitations before deciding whether another subscription is needed.

sections.heading: Generate the screens and connect the flow
paragraphs: Give the assistant the customer task, the information it can use, the output you want and the limits it must respect. OpenAI Academy’s small-business workshop calls these Goal, Context, Output and Boundary. They help you explain the request without needing technical language. The hypothetical garden-tidy exercise below applies that structure; it does not assume your chosen tool can generate working, clickable screens.

Check what the assistant actually returns. A screen specification describes the layout, words and behaviour. A static image shows an appearance but has no working controls. A clickable prototype connects screens so someone can follow a route. If the assistant supplies only copy, layouts, specifications or images, use them to assemble editable screens in an already-approved design or presentation tool.

subsections.heading: Copy and adapt this prompt
paragraphs: Replace the bracketed descriptions with your intended business, customer and task. The supplied sample details belong to the hypothetical garden-tidy example and are synthetic, not customer records.

Act as a design assistant for [small business and proposed offering]. Intended user: [customer]. Task: [one customer task]. For this hypothetical exercise, create a low-fidelity, mobile-first prototype with exactly three primary screens: (1) enter the necessary details, (2) review them and edit, and (3) view a simulated acknowledgement. Keep the layout simple and suitable for a narrow phone screen.

For this hypothetical garden-tidy example, use only these synthetic details: Sample Customer A; demo@example.com; service: one-off garden tidy; garden size: small; job note: weed beds and sweep paths. Include labelled fields, concise plain-English copy, a missing-required-field state and an invalid-email state within the relevant screen. Specify forward, edit/back and restart interactions. Use readable text and errors that do not rely on colour alone.

Do not create real accounts, send messages, store submissions, connect services, quote prices or promise availability. Label the final screen: Demo only—nothing has been sent. Output editable screens and an interaction map if supported; otherwise provide a screen specification and exact linking instructions. List assumptions, simulated behaviours and anything requiring human review. Do not invent customer findings.

subsections.heading: Connect the screens and check the preview
paragraphs: For the hypothetical garden-tidy flow, link the job-details screen to the review screen. From review, provide an edit action that returns to job details and a simulated submission action that opens the acknowledgement. Let the acknowledgement restart the demonstration. If the tool has not created those links, connect the buttons manually where supported, then follow each route in preview or presentation mode.
Links alone do not prove that form behaviour works. If the prototype cannot accept typed details, label that behaviour as simulated and record the limitation.

sections.heading: Walk through the prototype before showing it to anyone
paragraphs: Inspect the generated screens yourself rather than accepting the assistant’s claim that they work. Business.gov.au advises checking AI-generated information before relying on it. For this hypothetical garden-tidy prototype, start with the normal route using the supplied synthetic details: enter the request, review it and open the simulated acknowledgement. Check that necessary details are requested before review, the review matches the input and every button reaches its intended destination.

Then try the correction routes. Leave a required field blank, enter an invalid fictional email address, return from review to change the garden size, then restart the demonstration. Keep a short issue log recording the route, expected behaviour, observed behaviour and anything you simulated manually. A drawn error message does not demonstrate functioning validation. If the prototype cannot preserve edited values or respond to invalid input, record that limitation rather than treating the route as passed.

Read the copy alongside those interactions. Look for unexplained fields, missing instructions and promises about prices, availability or messages being sent that the demonstration cannot fulfil. Where “Continue” leaves the destination unclear, use a label such as “Review job details”. Check that the acknowledgement describes a simulation, not a real quote request or booking, and that returning to edit is easy to find.

Open a narrow mobile preview and inspect it for clipped content, readable text and enough spacing to distinguish adjacent buttons. Where the tool permits, try keyboard navigation and zoom, and check whether keyboard focus remains visible. Inspect field labels and make sure errors explain the problem in words rather than relying on colour alone. Mark checks the tool cannot support as “not testable here”. These are practical checks for this exercise, not a comprehensive accessibility audit, security assessment or proof of operational reliability.

Ask for a bounded revision, then repeat the affected route. For example, in this hypothetical prototype: “On the review screen, add an Edit job details action that returns to the entry screen; keep all other copy unchanged.” Check the revised copy and links yourself, and update the issue log with what changed, what remains unresolved and what is still simulated.

sections.heading: Draft a capped pilot before committing money
paragraphs: Plan a usability rehearsal with synthetic information, not a live quote-request service. For the hypothetical garden-tidy offering, invite willing participants who resemble the intended customer where feasible, explain that nothing will be submitted, and name a human reviewer who can check outputs and stop the exercise. The immediate question is whether people can complete and understand the proposed flow, not whether the business is ready to launch it.

Set the time and spending limits before inviting participants or buying tools. Record a comparable baseline for the current enquiry process, including customer effort and the owner's checking and correction work. MLAI's workflow-selection guide recommends observing the existing process and separating setup from recurring effort. If you have no comparable baseline, write “not measured” and collect it before claiming an improvement.

blocks.brief: In two short sentences, instruct readers to use synthetic inputs and never enter confidential or personal information into an unapproved tool; require human review of generated outputs. Keep the full warning here rather than repeating it in adjacent prose.
blocks.title: Keep real customer data out

props.text: Use synthetic inputs, and never enter personal or confidential information into an unapproved tool. Have a person review all generated copy and interactions before relying on them.

faq.rationale: The body answers the relevant beginner questions about tool capabilities, manual linking, synthetic data, prototype limitations, review and pilot decisions. No distinct unanswered questions justify a repetitive FAQ.

layout.rationale: Use a restrained layout built around the article's actual working materials: an inline reusable prompt, a concise pilot-scorecard table and three peer questions. One warning earns a decorative block because it appears at the point of data entry. Omit a step list because the prose already carries the four-phase sequence; omit audience cards because there is one reader; omit quotes because no supported counter-intuitive finding needs a separate spotlight. Honour feedback against generic resource and template CTAs by keeping the working aids on-page. The optional events link follows the completed task in ordinary conclusion prose. Do not plan the system-rendered hero, table of contents, references, disclaimer, company CTA, author bio or footer. No example-page statistics were supplied, so density follows the task and available evidence rather than an invented page-length target.
